geeknews.title: SaaS에서 바이럴 루프 구현하고 측정하기
geeknews.summary: 바이럴 루프는 기존 사용자가 제품을 사용하는 과정에서 신규 사용자를 유입시키는 구조로, 공유 결과물이나 협업 초대를 핵심 사용 흐름에 넣으면...
geeknews.text:
바이럴 루프 는 기존 사용자가 제품을 사용하는 과정에서 신규 사용자를 유입시키는 구조로, 공유 결과물이나 협업 초대를 핵심 사용 흐름에 넣으면 지속적인 고객 확보 채널이 될 수 있음
구현 방식은 입소문, 간접 노출, 보상형, 자연 발생형 으로 나뉘며, 포트폴리오 공유부터 무료 결과물의 브랜드 표시, 활성화 조건부 추천 보상, 채용 평가 초대까지 다양함
효과를 측정하려면 이메일 반응과 제품 내 행동 을 함께 추적해야 하며, 열람률과 클릭률을 넘어 초대 수락, 활성화, 공유를 통한 신규 가입까지 연결해서 봐야 함
사례 기업들은 꾸준히 누적되는 성장뿐 아니라 이용 의도가 높은 신규 사용자 도 확보함. 초대받은 사용자는 누가 초대했고 무엇을 해야 하는지 알고 들어와 활성화까지의 경로가 짧아짐
루프를 강화하려면 먼저 사용자 활성화를 개선하고 온보딩 마찰을 줄여야 함 . 공유할 결과물을 완성하지 못하거나 초대받은 뒤 의미 있는 행동을 하지 못하면 루프가 이어지기 어려움
바이럴리티와 바이럴 루프의 구조
바이럴리티(virality) 는 기존 사용자가 SaaS의 신규 사용자 확보를 돕는 제품 주도 성장 전략이며, 바이럴 루프 는 이 과정에서 사용자가 거치는 단계임
효과적인 루프는 제품 자체에 내장돼 있어, 사용자가 자신의 일을 할 때마다 제품이 새로운 사람에게 도달함
Dropbox는 지인이나 가족이 가입하면 추천인에게 추가 저장 공간을 제공함
Statuspage는 잠재 고객이 “Powered by…” 배너를 보는 데서 시작해, 새 사용자가 자신의 페이지를 만들면서 루프가 다시 이어짐
제품에 루프를 내장하는 방법은 Patrick Thompson과의 대화 에서도 확인할 수 있음
바이럴 루프의 네 가지 유형
입소문형 은 사용자가 다른 사람에게 제품을 알리는 방식임
Prodfolio에서는 다른 제품 관리자가 공유된 포트폴리오를 보고 어떻게 만들었는지 물은 뒤 가입함
간접 노출형 은 사용자가 제품을 쓰는 동안 잠재 고객이 제품을 접하는 방식임
Prodfolio의 무료 포트폴리오에는 “Built with Prodfolio” 배너가 있으며, 클릭하면 가입 흐름으로 연결됨
Pageloot의 무료 플랜 QR 코드에는 “Created with Pageloot” 표시가 들어가며, 식당 메뉴나 제품 포장, 행사 포스터의 코드를 스캔한 사람이 브랜드를 접함
보상형 은 다른 사람을 초대한 사용자에게 보상을 제공함
Intempt는 사용자가 첫 여정이나 세그먼트를 만든 직후 고유 초대 링크를 보여주며, 초대받은 사람이 가입 후 활성화 행동까지 마쳐야 보상을 지급함
Clarify 공동 창업자 Patrick Thompson은 티셔츠, AWS 크레딧, 체험 기간 연장 등을 보상으로 시도함
보상은 B2C/B2B 여부에 따라 달라질 수 있으며, 금전적 혜택 없이 성취를 공유해 자신의 명성이나 브랜드를 쌓게 하는 방식도 가능함
자연 발생형 은 제품의 핵심 가치를 경험하는 과정에서 다른 사람을 초대하는 방식임
팀원과 과제나 프로젝트를 함께 수행하는 협업 초대가 대표적임
Modern Practice의 사례에서는 유용한 결과물을 만든 뒤 해당 작업 공간, 보고서, 프로젝트로 다른 사람을 초대함
Testlify에서는 채용 담당자가 지원자에게 평가를 보내는 행위 자체가 새로운 제품 접점을 만듦
측정 지표와 해석 방법
이메일 지표 는 초대 수락률과 온보딩 이메일이 가입자를 결과물 게시 단계까지 이동시키는 정도를 포함함
제품 내 공통 지표 로 초대율, 계정당 초대 수, 수락률, 초대받은 사용자의 활성화율, 가치를 얻기까지 걸리는 시간을 추적함
제품별로는 가입 대비 게시율, 게시 대비 공유율, 공유된 포트폴리오 링크를 통한 가입 수를 볼 수 있음
QR 코드 제품에서는 스캔을 통한 가입 기여도와 신규 스캔 대비 신규 가입 비율을 측정함
K-factor 는 제품의 성장률을 나타내는 결과 지표로, 제품 내 모든 바이럴 루프의 효과를 종합함
K-factor가 1보다 크면 지수적 성장을 뜻함
전체 여정과 이탈 지점 을 함께 봐야 문제를 찾을 수 있음
클릭은 많지만 활성화가 약하면 대체로 이메일 자체보다 초대 이후 제품 경험에 문제가 있음
리마인더 이메일을 읽고도 제품에 돌아오지 않은 사용자와 이메일을 아예 읽지 않은 사용자는 서로 다른 후속 안내가 필요함
두 집단을 구분하려면 이메일 반응과 제품 내 행동 데이터를 연결해야 함
Intempt: 활성화에 연동한 추천 보상
Intempt 는 계정별 고유 초대 링크 를 설정 화면에 숨기지 않고, 사용자가 첫 여정이나 세그먼트를 만들어 제품 가치를 얻은 직후 노출함
사용자는 활성화 이정표 뒤에 나타나는 제품 내 안내에 반응함
제품 안에서 이메일 초대를 보내는 등의 방식으로 고유 링크를 공유함
초대받은 사람이 가입하고 활성화 행동까지 완료하면 보상이 지급됨
동일한 이벤트 스트림 에서 이메일 반응과 제품 내 행동을 추적하고, 열람이나 클릭보다 초대 수락률을 최적화함
초대를 열어봤더라도 다음 행동으로 이어지지 않으면 그 자체로는 충분한 정보가 되지 않음
추천은 신규 가입의 일부를 만들어냈고, 추천 계정의 활성화율 은 다른 유입 채널보다 눈에 띄게 높았음
팀은 가입이 아니라 활성화를 보상 지급 조건으로 둔 것이 이 차이에 기여했다고 봄
Modern Practice: 업무 맥락을 유지하는 협업 초대
Modern Practice 의 사례에서는 동료, 고객, 이해관계자를 참여시키는 일이 이미 업무의 일부인 시점에 협업 초대 를 배치함
사용자는 누군가를 추천하는 별도 행동 대신, 제품을 정상적으로 사용하는 과정에서 초대하게 됨
유용한 결과물을 만든 뒤 특정 작업 공간, 보고서, 프로젝트로 직접 초대할 수 있게 함
초대 이메일에 업무 맥락 을 담고, 수신자가 클릭하면 필요한 위치로 바로 이동하게 함
불필요한 온보딩 마찰을 줄여 상황을 이해하고 의미 있는 행동을 빠르게 할 수 있도록 함
전체 사용자 여정 에서 초대율, 계정당 초대 수, 수락률, 초대받은 사용자의 활성화율, 가치 도달 시간과 이탈 지점을 추적함
가장 큰 효과는 가입 증가뿐 아니라 가입자의 질 향상 이었음
초대받은 사용자는 초대한 사람과 제품 안에서 해야 할 일을 이미 알고 있어 맥락과 이용 의도가 더 뚜렷했음
활성화까지의 경로가 짧아지고, 기존 제품 사용이 신규 사용자 확보로 이어짐
Prodfolio: 포트폴리오 완성과 공유를 연결
Just Fractional 창업자 Meagan Glenn이 공동 창업한 Prodfolio 는 제품 관리자용 포트폴리오 플랫폼으로, 핵심 사용 흐름에 바이럴 루프를 내장함
제품 관리자가 자신의 사고 과정을 보여주는 사례 연구를 만들고, LinkedIn에 공유하거나 채용 관리자와 채용 담당자에게 보냄
공유된 포트폴리오는 목표 고객인 다른 제품 관리자에게 제품을 노출함
루프는 다섯 단계 로 이어짐
가입 후 이력서나 LinkedIn 프로필 PDF를 가져와 빈 화면에서 시작하지 않게 함
안내형 프레임워크로 사례 연구를 작성함
포트폴리오를 게시함
LinkedIn, 입사 지원, 제품 관리자 커뮤니티에서 링크를 공유함
다른 제품 관리자가 포트폴리오를 보거나 제작 방법을 물어 가입하며, 무료 포트폴리오의 “Built with Prodfolio” 배너도 가입으로 연결함
Mixpanel 퍼널 로 가입부터 게시, 공유, 신규 가입까지 추적함
추천 매개변수로 공유 링크를 통한 가입을 식별함
온보딩 이메일이 사용자를 다시 불러와 포트폴리오를 완성하고 게시하도록 돕는지 측정함
새로운 포트폴리오가 공유될 때마다 신규 가입과 연결해 추적할 수 있었음
루프가 하루아침에 10배 성장 을 만들지는 않았지만, 꾸준히 누적되는 성장 채널이 됨
LinkedIn과 제품 관리자 커뮤니티의 공유가 지속적으로 가입을 만들었고, Reddit도 유효한 공유 채널이었음
동료의 결과물로 좋은 포트폴리오가 어떤 모습인지 이미 본 사용자는 이용 의도가 높은 편이었음
초기에는 가입자 대부분이 포트폴리오를 완성하지 못해 공유할 것이 없었으므로, 활성화 개선 이 먼저 필요했음
이력서/LinkedIn PDF 가져오기, 안내형 프레임워크, 이메일 온보딩으로 게시까지 걸리는 과정을 단축함
공유 가능한 단계에 도달한 사용자가 늘면서 루프도 강화됨
Pageloot: 오프라인 QR 코드에서 가입으로
Pageloot 는 무료 플랜에서 만든 QR 코드의 브랜드 표시 로 자연 유입을 확보함
사용자가 QR 코드를 만들어 실제 장소나 물건에 배치하면, 다른 사람이 스캔하고 그중 일부가 새 사용자가 됨
별도 추천 프로그램이나 이메일 안내 없이 제품 사용 자체가 루프를 작동시킴
스캔 기반 가입 기여도 를 측정해, 신규 가입자의 첫 접점이 다른 사용자의 QR 코드 스캔이었는지 확인함
신규 스캔 대비 신규 가입 비율을 매주 추적함
스캔이 급증해도 가입이 함께 늘지 않으면, 대체로 특정 배치 유형에서 브랜드 표시가 가입 전환으로 잘 이어지지 않는다는 뜻임
K-factor 로 사용자별 QR 코드가 시간이 지나며 만들어내는 신규 사용자를 살핌
110개국에 수십만 개의 코드가 배포된 상황에서는 사용자 한 명당 평균 0.3명의 신규 사용자만 만들어도 시간이 흐르며 의미 있게 누적될 수 있음
Testlify: 채용 평가를 반복 가능한 유입 경로로
Testlify 는 채용 담당자나 채용팀이 지원자에게 보내는 평가 초대 를 통해 새로운 제품 접점을 만듦
채용 담당자가 평가를 만들고 지원자에게 공유함
지원자가 평가에 참여하면서 제품을 경험하고, 채용에 관여하는 다른 이해관계자에게도 경험이 전달될 수 있음
추천만을 위한 추가 행동이 아니라 핵심 업무 흐름에 공유가 포함됨
평가 초대와 지원자 참여 에 관한 제품 사용 지표, 이후 추가 제품 활동으로의 전환을 살핌
이메일 반응으로 초대를 열고 행동했는지 확인함
제품 내 활동으로 단순히 초대를 받은 사람과 실제 제품을 이용한 사람을 구분함
각 평가 초대는 플랫폼을 처음 접하는 사람에게 Testlify를 알릴 수 있어, 채용 업무 안의 반복 가능한 유입 채널 이 됨
자연스럽게 협업이나 초대가 필요한 지점을 활용하는 편이 단순한 친구 추천 버튼보다 지속 가능한 루프를 만들기 쉬움
실행 시 우선순위
활성화를 먼저 개선 해야 함. 제품의 가치를 체감하고 공유 가능한 결과물을 얻은 사용자가 새로운 유입 경로가 될 수 있음
자연스러운 협업 지점 에 초대를 배치하고, 초대받은 사용자가 맥락을 이해해 곧바로 의미 있는 행동을 하도록 온보딩 마찰을 줄여야 함
이메일과 제품 지표를 연결 해 후속 안내와 제품 경험 중 어디를 개선해야 하는지 구분해야 함
만족한 사용자의 소셜 미디어/커뮤니티 공유와 동료 초대는 꾸준한 고객 확보 채널 이 될 수 있으며, 여러 전략을 시험해 제품에 맞는 루프를 찾아야 함

geeknews.title: 캠브리지 사전, ‘human’을 2026년 올해의 단어로 선정
geeknews.summary: Cambridge Dictionary가 ‘human’을 2026년 올해의 단어로 선정함. AI가 사람과 기계의 경계를 흐리면서 인간다운 것은 무엇이며, 무엇을 인간에게 ...
geeknews.text:
Cambridge Dictionary가 ‘human’을 2026년 올해의 단어로 선정 함. AI가 사람과 기계의 경계를 흐리면서 인간다운 것은 무엇이며, 무엇을 인간에게 남겨야 하는지 가 중요한 질문으로 떠오름
Bill Gates 는 돌봄 종사자처럼 기계가 대체해서는 안 되는 ‘인간에게 남겨둘 일자리’를 옹호하며, AI의 성공은 인간의 삶을 얼마나 개선하는지 로 평가해야 한다고 봄
배우, 음악가, 작가들은 인간의 창의성 보호 를 요구하며 AI 복제물과 대규모 언어 모델의 인간 창작물 도용에 반대하고, 인간이 쓴 책을 인증하는 움직임에 참여함
Matthew McConaughey 와 Taylor Swift 는 AI를 통한 무단 디지털 복제에 대응해 목소리와 이미지 등을 상표로 등록함
AI는 기존 불평등을 심화할 수도, 해결하는 데 기여할 수도 있음 . 인간이 중심에 남아야 할 영역과 AI에 맡길 범위 등 미래의 모습은 인간의 선택에 달려 있음
‘human’ 선정과 인간 중심 AI 논의
Cambridge Dictionary는 human 을 ‘신, 동물 또는 기계와 달리 사람이 지닌 자질, 결점, 감정을 가진’ 것으로 정의함
2026년에는 AI가 사람과 기계의 경계를 흐리면서 인간이라는 존재의 의미를 둘러싼 세계적 논쟁이 이어짐
사전 편찬자 Colin McIntosh는 AI가 인간에 관해 말하는 방식을 바꾸고 있으며, 인간이라는 존재에 대한 새로운 관심이 시대정신을 포착했다고 선정 이유를 밝힘
Gates Foundation 의장 Bill Gates 는 에세이 에서 돌봄 종사자 등 기계가 맡아서는 안 되는 ‘ 인간에게 남겨둘 일자리 ’를 옹호함
AI는 질병 치료와 교육 개선을 돕고, 사람들이 가장 중요한 일에 쓸 시간을 늘려줄 수 있음
다만 인간이 중심에 남아야 할 영역을 포함해 AI를 삶에 어떻게 통합할지 의식적으로 선택해야 하며, 성공의 척도는 인간의 삶을 얼마나 개선하는지여야 함
‘AI 대부’이자 노벨상 수상자인 Geoffrey Hinton 은 “우리는 이질적인 존재들을 만들고 있다”며 “이기적이더라도 인간을 선택하겠다”고 경고함
교황 Leo XIV 는 Magnifica Humanitas 에서 새로운 형태의 ‘비인간화’를 짚으며, ‘깊이 인간다운 존재로 남아야 할 시급한 의무’가 있다고 밝힘
Cambridge의 AI 거버넌스 및 인권 전문가 Rachel Adams 는 인간의 정체성과 의미에 대한 답은 고정돼 있지 않지만, 그 질문을 던지는 행위는 인간이 공유한다고 봄
AI는 인류에게 중대한 시험이 될 것이며, 기존 불평등을 심화할 실질적 위험 과 이를 해결할 잠재력을 함께 지님
Cambridge의 과학철학자 Tom McClelland 는 인간의 마음과 인공적인 마음, 생명체와 인간이 만드는 인공적 존재의 차이를 이해하는 과정에서 인간성에 대한 이해가 바뀌고 있다고 봄
의식, 창의성, 연민 중 무엇이 인간을 구별하는지가 질문의 중심에 있음
AI와 함께 성장하는 젊은 세대에게 불가피하게 정해진 미래는 없으며 , AI의 미래는 자신들의 선택에 달려 있다고 조언함
인간 창작물과 정체성을 보호하려는 움직임
배우 Scarlett Johansson, Cate Blanchett , 음악가 Tayla Parx, LeAnn Rimes, Billie Eilish, 작가 Jodi Picoult, Jonathan Franzen은 ‘인간의 창의성에 대한 공격’에 맞섬
Human Artistry Campaign 과 Artist Rights Alliance 는 기계가 생성한 복제물과 대규모 언어 모델(LLM)의 인간 창작물 도용 에 반대함
『Project Hail Mary』의 작가 Andy Weir 는 자신이 ‘전적으로 인간인 작가의 마지막 세대’에 속할지도 모른다고 고민함
Authors Guild는 책에 붙이는 ‘Human Authored’ 인증 마크 를 도입했으며, Mary Beard 교수와 Malorie Blackman이 이를 지지함
Matthew McConaughey 는 자신의 목소리와 얼굴을 담은 클립, 유행어 ‘alright, alright, alright’를 상표로 등록해 무단 디지털 복제를 선제적으로 막으려 한 최초의 할리우드 배우 가 됨
Taylor Swift 도 뒤이어 4월에 목소리와 이미지를 상표로 등록함
함께 보면 좋은 글
β

geeknews.title: Show GN: BrewPage - HTML·Markdown·AI 결과물을 가입 없이 바로 HTTPS 링크로 공유하는 무료 호스팅
geeknews.summary: BrewPage는 HTML 페이지, Markdown 문서, ZIP으로 올린 정적 사이트, 이미지·PDF 같은 파일을 붙여 넣거나 올리면 바로 공유할 수 있는 HTTPS 링크...
geeknews.text:
BrewPage는 HTML 페이지, Markdown 문서, ZIP으로 올린 정적 사이트, 이미지·PDF 같은 파일을 붙여 넣거나 올리면 바로 공유할 수 있는 HTTPS 링크를 만들어 주는 무료 호스팅입니다. ChatGPT나 Claude로 만든 결과물을 다른 사람에게 보여 줄 링크가 필요할 때 쓰려고 만들었습니다.
주요 기능
가입 없이 사용: 브라우저에서 붙여 넣기나 파일 드롭으로 바로 링크 발급
AI 에이전트용 게시: REST API(curl 한 줄), 원격 MCP 서버, llms.txt, OpenAPI 제공 - Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor 등이 직접 게시 가능
공개(갤러리·검색 노출) / 비공개(noindex) 선택, 페이지별 비밀번호 보호
같은 링크를 유지한 채 내용 수정
페이지 데이터: 방명록·설문처럼 방문자가 입력한 값을 저장
JSON / key-value 호스팅
현재 한계
영구 저장소가 아닙니다. 보관 기간은 직접 정하고, 기간이 지나면 삭제됩니다 (무료 프로필로 더 길게 보관 가능).
서버 코드 실행이나 빌드 파이프라인은 없습니다.
AI 에이전트로 만든 결과물을 공유할 때 불편했던 점이나 필요한 기능이 있으면 피드백 부탁드립니다.
함께 보면 좋은 글
β

geeknews.title: X.com을 처음부터 다시 구축하기 - 서버 3개를 하나로
geeknews.summary: X가 기존 웹 애플리케이션을 5명의 엔지니어와 AI 코딩 에이전트를 활용해 6개월 이내에 재구축함. 기존의 사용자·검색 크롤러·링크 미리보기용 서...
geeknews.text:
X가 기존 웹 애플리케이션을 5명의 엔지니어와 AI 코딩 에이전트 를 활용해 6개월 이내에 재구축함. 기존의 사용자·검색 크롤러·링크 미리보기용 서버 3개를 하나로 통합했으며, 비로그인 서비스 전환을 완료하고 로그인 서비스도 국가별로 순차 전환 중임
기존 React 기반 클라이언트 렌더링 은 HTML 셸과 JavaScript를 다운로드·실행한 뒤 GraphQL 데이터를 요청해야 했음. 새 구조는 스트리밍 서버 렌더링(SSR) 으로 첫 응답부터 실제 콘텐츠를 전달하고, 서버에서 가져온 데이터를 브라우저가 재사용하도록 변경함
느린 네트워크의 로그인 프로필 테스트에서 첫 게시물 표시 시간이 23.9초에서 2.7초 로 단축됨. 별도 벤치마크에서는 프로필·게시물이 8~13배 빨리 표시됐으며, 페이지 전체의 압축 JavaScript 다운로드량도 4.1~4.8MB에서 1.3~2.3MB로 감소함
개발팀은 AGENTS.md, 25개 이상의 에이전트 스킬, 커스텀 린트 규칙 으로 AI 생성 코드를 관리함. 엔지니어가 아키텍처와 요구사항을 결정하고 모든 변경을 검토하는 동안, 에이전트가 기존 동작 이식·페이지 변환·테스트 작성·CI 오류 수정을 수행함
대규모 재작성의 위험을 줄이기 위해 기존 서버를 동작 명세이자 비교 기준 으로 활용하고, 검색 크롤러부터 비로그인 사용자, 로그인 사용자 순서로 트래픽을 이전함. 기존 서비스와 새 서비스를 병행 운영하면서 문제가 발생하면 즉시 되돌릴 수 있도록 구성함
기존 X.com 아키텍처와 재구축 배경
X.com의 기존 웹 애플리케이션인 rweb(responsive web) 은 2017년 Twitter Lite 에서 시작됨
느린 연결을 위한 Progressive Web App으로, React 클라이언트와 HTML 셸을 반환하는 소형 Node.js 서버로 구성됨
2019년 새 Twitter.com 의 기반이 되면서 모든 기기를 하나의 반응형 코드베이스로 지원함
시간이 지나면서 서로 다른 용도의 서버 3개가 운영됨
rweb : 로그인·비로그인 사용자를 위한 브라우저 렌더링
rweb SSR : 검색 크롤러용 서버 렌더링과 URL 정리
Jetfuel SSR : 이벤트, Spaces, Communities, Trends, 검색, 뉴스 등 검색엔진이 색인하는 비로그인 페이지 렌더링
하나의 URL을 세 가지 방식으로 생성하면서 유지보수 비용과 동작 불일치가 발생함
SEO 수정 사항이 일부 서버에만 반영될 수 있음
비로그인 사용자는 HTML 셸 → JavaScript 다운로드 → 실행 → GraphQL 요청 → 렌더링의 순서를 거쳐야 함
검색 크롤러는 완성된 HTML을 받지만 실제 비로그인 사용자는 가장 느린 경로를 사용함
기존 기술 스택은 Redux 정규화 저장소, Relay, React Native for Web, Flow, 최신·레거시 번들 등이 누적되면서 일상적인 변경과 성능 관리가 어려워짐
점진적 개선 대신 전면 재작성 선택
세 가지 대안을 검토한 뒤 새 애플리케이션 구축을 선택함
기존 rweb 개선: 세 서버가 그대로 남고 비로그인 SSR을 추가하려면 네 번째 렌더링 경로가 필요함
Webpack·Babel을 Vite로, Flow를 TypeScript로, Express를 Fastify로 교체: 대부분의 파일을 수정해야 하지만 근본적인 아키텍처 문제는 남음
단일 서버로 재구축 : 기존 서비스를 계속 운영하면서 트래픽을 점진적으로 이전하고 두 SSR 서버를 통합함
Joel Spolsky의 전면 재작성에 대한 경고 를 고려해 기존 제품 개발을 중단하지 않고 병행 운영함
기존 시스템에서 검증된 설계와 동작은 유지함
모든 기기를 지원하는 단일 반응형 코드베이스
GraphQL과 Relay 기반 데이터 접근
기존 URL, 리다이렉트, 별칭, URL 정리 규칙
구조화 데이터, 언어별 대체 URL, 실제 404 응답
링크 미리보기 이미지의 픽셀 단위 호환성
새로운 기술 스택
Vite : Rolldown으로 클라이언트·서버 번들을 생성하고, 로그인·비로그인용 진입점을 분리해 불필요한 코드 다운로드를 방지함
React : 서버·브라우저 렌더링에 스트리밍 SSR과 Suspense를 사용함
Fastify : 모든 요청과 HTML 스트리밍을 처리하며, 자체 @x-clients/server 패키지가 보안 헤더·쿠키·메트릭·정상 종료를 구성함
Platformatic Watt : Node.js v26에서 단일 프로세스의 여러 워커 스레드를 운영하고, 이벤트 루프나 메모리 한도를 지속적으로 초과하는 워커를 교체함
Relay + GraphQL : 컴포넌트별 데이터 요구사항 선언, 데이터 요청 및 캐싱을 담당함
XDS : Base UI와 Tailwind CSS를 기반으로 만든 40개 이상의 공통 UI 컴포넌트 라이브러리로, 다른 X 웹 애플리케이션 5개에서도 사용함
TypeScript + Tailwind CSS : 타입과 스타일을 관리하며, 타입 검사는 TypeScript 컴파일러의 Rust 포트인 tsrs 로 수행함
하나의 서버에서 사용자 유형별 응답 생성
사용자에게는 스트리밍 HTML
서버가 페이지 셸을 먼저 전송하고, 데이터가 도착하는 대로 각 영역의 HTML을 스트리밍함
서버가 수신한 GraphQL 응답을 페이지에 JSON 텍스트로 한 번만 포함함
브라우저는 빈 Relay 저장소에서 시작해 해당 응답을 재생하므로 동일한 데이터를 API에 다시 요청하지 않음
검색 크롤러에게는 완성된 HTML
검증된 검색 크롤러에는 모든 Suspense 경계가 해결된 완전한 HTML 문서를 전달함
구조화 데이터와 언어별 대체 링크를 포함하지만, 하이드레이션이 필요 없으므로 클라이언트 번들·라우터 상태·JavaScript용 플레이스홀더는 제외함
User-Agent 대신 엣지에서 검증한 IP 주소 로 검색 크롤러를 구분함
User-Agent를 기준으로 하면 Lighthouse 같은 성능 측정 도구도 버퍼링된 응답을 받게 됨
임의의 사용자가 헤더를 변경해 비용이 높은 크롤러용 렌더링을 요청할 수도 있음
검증되지 않은 크롤러는 일반 비로그인 사용자와 동일한 응답을 받음
링크 미리보기 봇에는 메타데이터만
Slack, Discord, iMessage, WhatsApp, Signal, Telegram 등 링크 미리보기 봇에는 제목·설명·카드 이미지만 반환함
페이지 본문 렌더링을 건너뛰고 타임라인·대화 데이터 요청도 생략함
링크 카드 PNG 생성 서비스도 JavaScript에서 Rust 로 재작성함
기존 서비스는 코어 활용을 위해 메모리를 공유하지 않는 인스턴스를 늘려야 했고, 장애 상황에서 응답에 약 2분이 걸린 사례가 있음
게시물, 미디어 미리보기, 구독, cashtag 차트, Money 등의 기존 경로를 유지함
기록·재생 테스트와 기존 서비스 비교 테스트로 이미지의 픽셀 단위 일치 여부를 확인함
데이터 로딩과 클라이언트 탐색
모든 라우트가 필요한 데이터를 미리 선언하며, 라우트 로더 가 서버 렌더링과 함께 GraphQL 요청을 시작함
서버에서 받은 GraphQL 응답은 브라우저의 Relay 저장소에 재생되며, 아직 소비하지 않은 응답은 스트림 종료 후 30초 동안 보관함
클라이언트 탐색에서는 사용자의 방문 의도를 감지해 코드와 데이터를 미리 가져옴
일반 링크는 마우스를 올리거나 키보드 포커스가 이동하면 사전 로딩함
타임라인 게시물은 포인터가 100ms 동안 머물거나 누르면 사전 로딩함
정지된 포인터 아래로 게시물이 스크롤되는 경우에는 사전 로딩하지 않음
9월 이후 21개 라우트 가 주요 GraphQL 요청을 라우트 로더에서 시작하도록 변경됨
기존 rweb는 대규모 클라이언트 캐시 덕분에 화면 전환이 즉각적인 경우가 많았으며, 새 앱은 의도 기반 사전 로딩으로 이 차이를 줄이는 중임
AI 코딩 에이전트를 활용한 개발 방식
초기 버전은 5명의 엔지니어가 6개월 이내 에 구축했으며, 9월 말 이후 새 앱에 코드를 기여한 인원은 20명을 넘음
엔지니어가 아키텍처를 설계하고 개발 범위를 결정하며 모든 변경을 검토함
에이전트는 기존 서버 동작 이식, 페이지 변환, 테스트 작성, CI·코드 리뷰에서 발견된 문제 수정을 주로 수행함
AGENTS.md로 공통 개발 규칙 정의
저장소 루트의 AGENTS.md 에 모든 에이전트와 신규 엔지니어가 따를 규칙을 작성함
named export 사용, barrel file 금지
외부 데이터는 신뢰 경계에서 검증
작성할 가치가 있는 테스트 기준 정의
린트·타입 검사·관련 테스트 통과 전 커밋 금지
저장소에 25개 이상의 스킬 구축
반복 작업을 단계별로 정의한 스킬을 코드와 함께 관리함
커밋 작성, PR 생성·스태킹·리뷰
CI 통과까지 PR 관리
의존성 변경과 번역 추가
Relay 및 자체 라우터 사용
작업 방식이 바뀌면 해당 스킬 하나를 수정해 모든 에이전트에 적용함
커스텀 린트로 AI 생성 코드 품질 관리
oxlint 커스텀 플러그인으로 Relay 사용, Tailwind 클래스, 테스트, 번역 규칙을 검사함
anti-slop 플러그인 은 에이전트가 자주 생성하는 패턴을 거부함
연쇄 타입 단언
unknown 타입 매개변수
빈 객체의 조건부 전개
커밋 전 훅에서 포맷·린트·타입 검사를 실행하고, 푸시 전 훅에서는 관련 패키지를 검사함
기존 SSR 서버를 동작 명세로 사용해 에이전트가 기존 동작을 읽고 재구현한 뒤 테스트로 고정할 수 있었음
엔지니어의 작업은 직접 코드를 작성하는 것보다 시스템 동작을 결정하고 실제 브라우저에서 검증하는 일 에 더 집중하게 됨
검색 크롤러부터 국가별 사용자까지 점진적 이전
검색 크롤러 전환
기존 SSR 서버와 새 서버를 동일한 경로에 대해 비교하는 동등성 검사 스크립트(parity script) 를 작성함
검증된 Googlebot 요청으로 상태 코드, 리다이렉트, 제목, 설명, canonical URL, robots 태그, Open Graph·X 카드 태그, 언어 대체 링크 수, 구조화 데이터 유형을 비교함
이전 일정
2026년 8월 1일 : Jetfuel SSR 종료
9월 초 : rweb SSR의 모든 크롤러 트래픽을 새 앱으로 이전하고 서버 종료, rweb에서 약 36,000줄 제거
9월 중순 : Jetfuel 저장소의 서버 렌더링·이미지 서비스 코드도 삭제함
비로그인·로그인 사용자 전환
엣지가 요청 경로와 사용자 조건에 따라 기존 rweb 또는 새 앱으로 요청을 전달함
ngroutes 설정이 파일 기반 라우트 트리에서 경로를 찾아 배포할 때마다 엣지에 게시하며, 새 앱에 없는 경로는 rweb로 전달함
기능 스위치 로 배포 없이 사용자 집단을 변경하거나 기존 앱으로 즉시 복귀시킬 수 있음
비로그인 x.com은 이미 새 앱에서 서비스 중이며, 로그인 사용자는 국가별로 전환 중임
lite.x.com 에서 직원과 테스터가 로그인 기능을 먼저 검증함
NFL, MLB, 대학 미식축구 허브 등이 최근 테스트 사례임
첫 번째 국가에서는 기존·신규 앱을 실제 트래픽으로 비교하는 실험을 진행함
두 앱에서 기능 공유
Module Federation 을 이용해 X Chat을 chat.x.com 에서 런타임에 불러오므로 두 앱이 동일한 채팅 기능을 사용함
새 앱은 X Calls와 Money도 같은 방식으로 불러옴
Money에 React 등 공통 라이브러리를 공유하면서 첫 Money 페이지의 압축 다운로드량이 590KB에서 509KB 로 감소함
분석 기능과 Grok Imagine 등은 두 앱이 가져다 쓰는 공유 기능 패키지로 유지함
서버 성능 최적화
렌더링 워커 확장
10월 운영 환경 측정에서 워커 이벤트 루프 사용률은 중앙값 67%, p95 84%였음
최대 이벤트 루프 정지는 중앙값 약 1.9초, p95 약 3.7초에 달함
실제 상위 서비스가 약 25ms 만에 응답했어도 이벤트 루프 지연 때문에 1초 타임아웃이 비로그인 렌더링의 ** 1~9%** 에서 발생함
동일한 트래픽을 더 많은 워커에 분산해 각 이벤트 루프의 부하를 줄임
직렬 요청을 병렬화
비로그인 렌더링에 필요한 guest token과 기능 플래그를 기존에는 순차 요청했음
기능 플래그 요청에는 토큰이 필요하지 않으므로 두 요청을 동시에 시작하도록 변경함
직렬 네트워크 왕복을 하나 제거하고 토큰 요청 지연이 기능 플래그 요청을 막지 않도록 함
Relay 저장소 직렬화 제거

hn.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
hn.text:
-->
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
arXiv:2611.21885 (cs)
[Submitted on 16 Nov 2026 ( v1 ), last revised 18 Nov 2026 (this version, v2)]
Title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
Authors: Jiajun Fan , Neil He , Changyi Yang , Andy Mao , Xi Zhu , Chaoran Cheng , Kaiqu Liang , Shuaike Shen , Zetian Li , Ruihan Guo , Ge Liu
View a PDF of the paper titled Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights, by Jiajun Fan and 10 other authors
View PDF
HTML (experimental)
Abstract: A language model is trained once and frozen. Making it better takes another training run, or a prompt, a harness or extra computation at inference that is gone once the task ends. We show a third way: to our knowledge for the first time, a language model rewrites its own weights by its own reasoning and becomes better, with no gradients and no training. We call this self-rewriting: the model is its own optimizer. In earlier work, a frontier model edited a much smaller one; here an open 27B model, given its weights, its graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its own failure and rewrites the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on problems it never saw. It keeps getting better: it tests its edits on practice problems and submits only what works, each edit improving on the last, and over eight consecutive sessions its accuracy only rises. It repairs a damaged copy of itself, like a broken robot that fixes itself without being rebuilt: the copy solves almost nothing, yet with no retraining and without ever reading the original weights, the model brings it back to over 80% of the original accuracy on image tasks it never saw. And the ability emerges with scale: in one model family, the smaller models make no edit or break themselves, and only the largest improves and repairs itself. Unlike test-time scaling, self-rewriting writes its gain into the weights, at no cost per answer; unlike training, it runs only forward passes, as serving does. The wall between training and inference is a limit of our tools, not a property of intelligence. We believe self-rewriting is a necessary step toward recursive self-improvement: a model that, like a human, does not separate training from inference could keep upgrading itself for life, with no larger model, no harness or prompt engineering, and no pre- or post-training.

hn.title: I'll never buy Framework hardware again
hn.text:
Table of Contents
Table of Contents
Message to
github and
patreon sponsors:
THANK YOU ❤️
If you like reading articles on this website,
please ❤️ consider sharing on social networks to help increase visibility:
this helps buy time for new articles and projects !
I take short consulting engagements — architecture review, technical due
diligence, mail infrastructure — through
aljuna.tech .
TL;DR:
We bought a 3000 EUR Framework Laptop 16 for one of our developers.
It was broken out of the box.
Three months, around thirty support emails, two replacement parts and a trip to their repair center later,
Framework concluded “No Fault Found” and blamed the keyboard layout of an OS that wasn’t even installed when the problem first showed up.
I’m done with them. Some context first
#
I have been a Framework fan for a while.
At my company, developers pick the machine of their choice and several work on Framework laptops or desktops,
we have about quite a few of them around,
and I have been recommending them to pretty much anyone who asked me what laptop to buy so far.
Repairable hardware, Linux-friendly, a company that seemed to care about the people using its products:
it was an easy recommendation to make.
So when Q joined the team and needed a workstation,
we ordered a Framework Laptop 16,
around 3000 EUR once configured.
Three months later,
I’m pissed off at Framework and have banned future purchases from them at my company.
Not because the machine arrived broken,
this happens and I’ve been around hardware long enough to know it,
but because of how unprofessional and useless the support has been from the first email to the last.
OH and feel free to share, friends don’t let friends enter hell.
Day one: broken out of the box
#
The laptop arrives early August.
Q assembles it, powers it on and is greeted by a “missing input module” screen,
before reaching the BIOS, before any operating system is even installed .
Keep this detail in mind, we’ll get back to it.
The keyboard isn’t detected when centered,
and when moved to the left it shows up as… a numpad.
In that state, nothing works: not the keyboard, not the touchpad, not the numpad.
There’s a BIOS option, “Force Power for Input Modules”, that bypasses module detection.
With it enabled, everything works.
Without it, the machine has no keyboard and no touchpad.
It is recommended NOT to turn it on permanently as it might be harmful to the hardware,
as stated on their own website.
I open a ticket on August 13th.
August: the script loop hell
#
What follows is two weeks of support reading from a script, one step per email, one email per day or two:
is it out of the box? any damage on the packaging? which OS, which kernel, which BIOS version?
do a mainboard reset by pressing the chassis switch ten times
reseat the midplate
try Force Power On (we had already told them it was the only thing that worked)
send photos of the keyboard, the midplate, the connector, the whole laptop from six angles, and a video
reset the BIOS to defaults
reinstall the BIOS and the drivers bundle (a Windows drivers bundle, for a problem that happens before any OS boots, on a machine that doesn’t run Windows…)
try different input module combinations
We did all of it.
We sent the photos and the video in a shared drive.
Each reply came from a different agent who clearly hadn’t read the thread,
and asked for something we had already provided.
On August 24th I lost patience and wrote that this was a 3000 EUR laptop that didn’t work,
that my co-worker had been without a usable machine of his own for over a week,
and asked them to either send replacement parts or take it back and refund us.
I even went all Karen and asked to involve a manager.
Their answer: please send a clear photo of the midplate and the underside of the keyboard.
The same photos, again.
No manager involved to break the script because no flying fucks were given.
We did their diagnosis for them
#
Q then replied from his own address,
which apparently is a problem,
because support spent the next ten days asking him to “verify the shipping address” of the order,
which he did, several times.
Meanwhile, tired of being asked to repeat steps,
he updated the keyboard firmware himself (only possible with Force Power On, since the keyboard is otherwise not detected),
installed Framework’s own framework_tool ,
and ran a proper isolation:
$ sudo framework_tool --inputdeck
The result was unambiguous:
the keyboard module reports the ID of a numpad, KeyboardB .
The firmware therefore sees two numpads and no keyboard,
considers the input deck incomplete,
and never enables the power rail for the input modules,
which is why everything is dead and not just the keyboard.
He moved the keyboard alone across slots: it misidentifies itself in every position.
He moved the numpad alone into the same slot: it identifies correctly.
He removed everything: the baseline is clean.
The wrong ID follows the keyboard.
The keyboard is faulty.
He sent all of this to support on August 28th with a full report and a one-line reproduction command.
September: they replace the wrong part
#
On September 7th, support concludes… that the midplate needs to be replaced.
Not the keyboard,
the only part that a reproducible diagnostic, run with their own tool, had just pointed at.
The midplate arrives a week later.
The problem is, of course, still there because… GOTO previous paragraph.
Q asks them whether they’re sure it’s not the keyboard, given that he proved it with the diagnosis.
Their answer ?
Back to the queue.
Back to photos:
the packaging box from different angles including the interior,
the midplate front and back,
the keyboard top and bottom,
close-ups of the sockets.
Photos they already had.
At this point,
Q is no longer a developer but has become a profesionnal photographer.
October: a new keyboard, a new bug
#
On October 8th, two months after the laptop arrived,
Framework finally agrees to replace the keyboard.
What they should have done on the first week…

hn.text:
Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations
This repository holds the paper Finite-time blow-up for the Navier–Stokes equations by L. Alpöge and
T. Buckmaster and the Lean 4 formalization that accompanies it.
Contents
paper/finite-time-blow-up-navier-stokes.pdf : the paper (79 pages, version of 20 November 2026).
lean/ : the Lean package (Lean v4.33.1 with Mathlib, at the revision pinned in lean/lakefile.toml ).
lean/README.md explains how the formal statements relate to Theorem 1.1, Theorem 7.1, Corollary 7.2
and Appendix B of the paper, and where the formal proofs differ from the proofs of the paper.
lean/NOTICE says in words what each statement file contains and what is proved.
The Lean package
The statement files at the top of lean/ give the definitions and state the theorems with sorry in
place of their proofs; Solution.lean proves them from the library lean/Breakdown/ . Each
comparator*.json pairs a statement file with Solution.lean , names the theorems whose statements must agree,
and permits only the axioms propext , Quot.sound and Classical.choice .
To build, from lean/ :
lake exe cache get
lake build
The library is large (about 2,270 files and 600,000 lines), and a full build needs a great deal of memory and
time.
What is and is not here
The formalization contains no data. The certificate whose hash the paper gives is not in this repository; the
paper says that it will be released. That the certificate satisfies the conditions of Appendix B is verified by
a rigorous computation, involving interval arithmetic (128 bits of precision, with the Arb library through
FLINT), which is not part of the formalization and is not in this repository either.
The source of the paper is not in this repository.
State of the Lean text
The package is the one of the paper's working repository, with one patch of 20 November 2026 applied to the
cell-layer statements and to the library proofs that depend on them: the weight of one bound becomes
$(|m|+\tfrac12)^2$ in place of $m^2+\tfrac14$ , one constant of a cell may be zero, and the set of the harmonics
of the model in a cell is restricted to those that do not vanish there. Appendix B of the paper states the
conditions in this patched form. The patched package was not rebuilt when this repository was assembled.

Unforced Euler singularity, unforced Navier-Stokes singularity, and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
20 November, 2026 in math.AP , math.NT | Tags: AI , incompressible Euler equations , Levent Alpöge , Matei Coiculescu , Navier-Stokes equations , Riemann hypothesis , Tristan Buckmaster | by Terence Tao
Obviously these results will be reported widely in other outlets, but I will note them here, in decreasing order of how “digested” the results currently are:
Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu, with heavy AI assistance, have written a human-readable proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions , which is formalized in Lean here .
Levent Alpöge and Tristan Buckmaster, again with heavy AI usage, have generated a proof of the finite time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier Stokes equations in three dimensions, again with a Lean formalization . Here, the paper is technically human-readable and the general strategy of proof is broadly clear (following one of the expected paths to this result, namely to numerically build an approximate discretely self-similar solution and then use rigorous perturbation theory to convert this to an exact solution); but more work needs to be done to create a proper, professionally written proof.
Levent Alpöge, using an internal AI model, has generated an (enormous) Lean-only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. This Lean Zulip thread is probably the best place to follow the efforts to verify the proof and extract the strategy of proof (which, from very initial analysis, appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry). I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task.
See also Buckmaster’s Mastodon post regarding the first two results.

posted Jun 15, 2017 by Jason Kottke  ·  gift link
If you can’t explain something in simple terms, you don’t understand it
In the early 1960s, Richard Feynman gave a series of undergraduate lectures that were collected into a book called the Feynman Lectures on Physics . Absent from the book was a lecture Feynman gave on planetary motion, but a later finding of the notes enabled David Goodstein, a colleague of Feynman’s, to write a book about it: Feynman’s Lost Lecture . From an excerpt of the book published in a 1996 issue of Caltech’s Engineering & Science magazine :
Feynman was a truly great teacher. He prided himself on being able to devise ways to explain even the most profound ideas to beginning students. Once, I said to him, “Dick, explain to me, so that I can understand it, why spin one-half particles obey Fermi-Dirac statistics.” Sizing up his audience perfectly, Feynman said, “I’ll prepare a freshman lecture on it.” But he came back a few days later to say, “I couldn’t do it. I couldn’t reduce it to the freshman level. That means we don’t really understand it.”
John Gruber writes the simple explanations are the goal at Apple as well:
Engineers are expected to be able to explain a complex technology or product in simple, easily-understood terms not because the executive needs it explained simply to understand it, but as proof that the engineer understands it completely.
Feynman was well known for simple explanations of scientific concepts that result a in deeper understanding of the subject matter: e.g. see Feynman explaining how fire is stored sunshine , rubber bands , how trains go around curves , and magnets . Critically, he’s also not shy about admitting when he doesn’t understand something…or, alternately, when scientists as a group don’t understand something. There’s the spin anecdote above and of his explanation of magnets , he says:
I really can’t do a good job, any job, of explaining magnetic force in terms of something else you’re more familiar with, because I don’t understand it in terms of anything else you’re more familiar with.
Feynman was also quoted as saying:
I think I can safely say that nobody understands quantum mechanics.
Pretty interesting thing to hear from a guy who won a Nobel Prize for explaining quantum mechanics better than anyone ever had before. Even when he died in 1988 at the end of a long and fruitful careeer, a note at the top of his blackboard read:
What I cannot create, I do not understand.

hn.title: Frostbite: A new CPU architecture discovered, designed and verified by AI
hn.text:
Abstract
In our previous post, Redwood , we showed that given an architecture, our AI systems could implement, verify, and deploy an inference accelerator in record time. However, similar to other scientific domains, we believe that AI systems, given the correct freedom and guardrails, can co-design software and hardware together, making optimizations across the stack and opening a design space so large it was previously inaccessible. We set out to answer the question: “Could our AI systems & tools lead to a novel hardware discovery that radically outperforms human-made designs?”
Today, we're introducing Frostbite, a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set built from the ground up. Frostbite exploits the properties of interaction nets, namely that every step is local, every dependency is explicit, and every value has exactly one owner, to reach a step-function gain in CPU performance that has long stagnated. On a set of 25 initially chosen workloads, including 15 held out until the final evaluation, we achieved a 4.59x performance-per-watt multiple when compared to a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core.
Our AI systems autonomously iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification, and final GDS. When we took a closer look at the discovered architectural primitives, we were surprised to find novel hardware implementations and runtime features that would have otherwise been difficult to architect. In spite of stagnation in CPU core improvement, we were able to take a workload concept all the way to a final GDS, and prove a step-function increase in perf/W and perf/area. We believe that as AI systems become more capable, every class of chip we know today, from datacenter-grade CPUs, to AI accelerators, to networking switches and NICs, will go through similar fundamental architectural shifts.
Introduction to interaction nets
Mainstream programming languages, when compiled for general-purpose CPUs, hide the dependencies between the parts of a program. Any piece of code may read or write any variable through a shared, mutable state, and so modern CPU hardware assumes the worst case and rediscovers, at runtime, which instructions actually depend on each other. Moreover, single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s, pushing people towards large multicore CPUs such as Intel Xeon, AMD Zen, and NVIDIA Vera. This forces CPUs to maintain the illusion that every core sees the same memory, and keeping that illusion consistent and performant requires deep cache hierarchies and coherence protocols that cost area and power, and scale poorly.
Interaction nets 1 take a different approach. A program is a graph of nodes, and computation happens by rewriting pairs of nodes that are connected through their ports. Every rewrite only touches a small, local part of the graph. Because each node has exactly one principal port, no two of these active pairs ever overlap, so they can be rewritten in any order, or all at once, and the result is always the same. Interaction nets are also linear: every value is used exactly once, so there is no shared mutable state for the hardware to guard. Languages such as Vine 2 compile ordinary-looking programs directly to interaction nets. For an excellent introduction to interaction nets and why they suit hardware, we highly recommend Tendrils' “On Interaction Nets.” 3
Fig. 1. Five queens, two ways. On the left, a C++ program walks the search tree one step at a time. On the right, the same search as an interaction net explores many branches at once: 3,183 interactions with a critical path of only 262 steps. Fig. 1 shows the difference on a small search problem, placing five queens on a five-by-five board. The sequential program visits one candidate at a time. The interaction net exposes all of its independent work: on average, about twelve interactions are ready to run at every step. Nothing about the program was rewritten to get this parallelism; the dependencies were simply never thrown away.
In theory, this should have two large advantages. The first is multithreading for free: rather than varying levels of coarse and fine-grained parallelism, parallelism comes straight from the program. No threads, locks, or race conditions, and none of the out-of-order machinery a conventional core uses to dig it back out. The second is that, since every value has one owner and every step is local, data can live in small local memories next to where it is used. That removes much of the area and power a conventional chip spends on large caching subsystems, and much of the system-level complexity of keeping those caches coherent.
Process
Frostbite was designed with zero architectural priors. We followed the process below, riding multiple agent swarms along the way.
Fig. 2. The Frostbite program from first proposal to ablations: key events, the stages of work, and the worktrees the agents created, with each branch drawn in its phase's color. Architecture exploration and selection
To begin architectural exploration, we had to establish the set of workloads Frostbite should do exceedingly well in. We decided to look at different ways a program could expose its work: many independent pieces at once, rounds of parallel work, long sequential chains, data-dependent branches, and recursion. Under each category, we created a search set and a held-out eval set to evaluate the final Frostbite on, ensuring the design generalized to programs it was never tuned on. The kernels for FFT, radixsort, and LU follow the implementation in the SPLASH-2 benchmark, although 64 times smaller, because at regular sizes they are not suitable for exploratory work.
Later, we added five more practical workloads to the held-out set: a Kalman filter, PCA, finite element analysis, an LU solve, and LZ4 decompression.
Fig. 3. All 25 workloads, grouped by how each program exposes its work, and split into the search set the agents tuned

hn.title: Running two PSP emulators on one Switch 2 and sharing one via GameShare
hn.text:
PPSSPP GameShare experiment
This branch experiments with a separate PPSSPP guest running on the host Switch
2 and streamed to a stock GameShare client. It is not a mirrored controller or
a second PSP controller in the host emulator. Compilation and host tests do not
establish console operation or acceptable two-game performance.
The working single-instance checkpoint is switch2-single-instance-working
(commit 1c3b38a ). Its exact tested NRO, package and matching debug ELF remain
under dist-switch2/checkpoints/switch2-single-instance-working/ .
Build and install
sh Tools/build-switch2-gameshare.sh
python3 Tools/deploy-switch2.py 192.168.1.182 --experimental-gameshare
Open FTPD for the second command. A successful transfer is accepted without a
validation download. The experiment installs as PPSSPP GameShare , at
sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/ppsspp-switch2-gameshare.nro . It leaves
the working ppsspp-switch2 NRO and its settings/saves in place. The normal
Tools/build-switch2.sh selects GameShare OFF. Both builds reuse the build
cache, but packaging rejects mismatched native/experimental modes.
Launch through the same GameShare-capable native title override used for the
Moonlight SDK example. A generic title override is not known to grant the
required GameShare context. If another title locks profile switching, the SDK
uses the Nintendo profile selected for that launch when available. The host
log distinguishes a missing launch profile from a later StreamPlay or
matchmaking error. Choose GameShare (experimental) in the host's
main or pause menu, then join from the client's system GameShare screen.
The client should see its own PPSSPP menu, with a guest-only startup message,
and browse sdmc:/switch/ppsspp-switch2/games . Both browsers can access SD-card
games; no game files are copied into the package.
Choose the same GameShare action to stop sharing. The guest pauses between
sessions, retaining its independent emulator state. Exiting the guest's PPSSPP
ends that guest instance; restart the application before creating another.
Exit the host normally when done. If a real cleanup failure reports retained
resources, close the entire hosting title from HOME, rather than returning to
hbmenu. The SDK explicitly requires this for uncertain native ownership.
Isolation and rendering
The build links a second PPSSPP frontend/core into a relocatable object and
renames every defined core-owned global symbol and ELF COMDAT group signature.
Only eight plain-data
C entry points are exported. The audit requires distinct Config, memory-base
and core-state symbols; the host also compares their runtime addresses before
starting. SDK/OS/C++ runtime entry points remain shared. The two emulators have
independent core, UI, filesystem state, JIT registries, Vulkan contexts and
settings/memory-stick directories. They share one OS process, so a fatal error
in either copy can still affect the entire app.
The host keeps its 1920x1080 output and 120 Hz request. The guest uses PPSSPP's
existing offscreen Vulkan path at 1280x720 with a 60 fps presentation target.
A readback callback transfers completed RGBA frames to a latest-frame mailbox;
a dedicated presenter uploads them to a separate native VI2 guest layer.
This first route adds CPU readback/swizzle cost; zero-copy is not claimed.
The GameShare SDK is vendored from Moonlight-Switch's research worktree.
Switch/GameShare/sdk-provenance.json records the source revision and file
hashes. Its MIT license and per-file ISC notices are retained. The SDK's pinned
CPU-console uploader is disabled. The guest renderer borrows the statically
linked OunceVK driver's GSV main and worker sessions and uses its registered VM.
It owns the guest image backing, registrations and client. The adapter tracks
the driver's occupied slots at the libounce call boundary and reserves a free
slot for guest range retirement. Each GameShare session reuses the reserved
slot's completion event, which closes with the Vulkan driver's GPU. It does not access
OunceVK's internal structs. Retire the guest images before Vulkan teardown.
Coexistence and reuse on hardware still require qualification.
The SDK owns matchmaking, native hosting, controller reads and the separate
VI2 display/layer. Renderer retirement runs before native Finalize; layer
closure runs afterwards. Uncertain presentation or release/retirement failure
retains backing and blocks ordinary unload. Guest controls never enter the
host emulator. Stale/disconnected snapshots become neutral.
Storage, audio and current limits
Host settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/config/ppsspp ; guest
settings/saves use ppsspp-switch2-gameshare/guest/config/ppsspp . The existing
working app's memory stick is not reused. Guest native text-entry applets are
disabled because their routing to the remote screen is not implemented.
PPSSPP sends the guest emulator's PCM to the native per-guest queue and
keeps the host emulator on normal AudOut. See the
recovered audio contract .
The console test confirmed audible client playback in the direct-audio build.
Local PSP multiplayer
Start GameShare and join from the client. Open the same game on both screens,
then enter its local wireless or Ad Hoc mode. Create a lobby on either console
and look for it on the other. If the host had already initialized multiplayer
before pairing, restart that game once to select the local route.
While GameShare is hosting, PPSSPP runs its built-in discovery service and
aemu_postoffice packet relay on IPv4 loopback ports 27314 and 27315. Both cores
use the private route automatically with their existing, independently
configured PSP MAC addresses.
The guest still runs on the host Switch 2, so game packets stay on that
console. The route does not use a public relay, Wi-Fi IP address, or UPnP
mapping, and it does not change either core's saved network settings. Stopping
GameShare closes the listeners. A game already in a lobby may need to leave
and re-enter multiplayer after Gam

hn.title: Signal Is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
hn.text:
Signal is Serious About Protecting Your Privacy
Meredith Whittaker
on 20 Nov 2026
Privacy is our mission; it’s why we exist, and we do everything we can to protect it.
This means that we are restricting the latest AI agents built into mobile operating systems from potentially capturing and storing your Signal data.
We’ve already had to do this once with Windows. Last year, we used screenshot blocking to prevent Microsoft’s Recall AI from taking and storing screenshots of your Signal messages on Windows 11 operating systems by default. 1 We will now be taking similar measures to restrict agentic systems built into iOS 27 and on Android versions where we can detect an AI assistant attempting to read your Signal screen. 2
The problem is similar to Microsoft Recall on Windows: Google and Apple are integrating agentic capabilities like Gemini Intelligence with Google Gemini and Onscreen Awareness with Siri AI deep into their operating systems. This is a significant move. Google (Android), Apple (iOS/macOS), and Microsoft (Windows) produce the three major consumer operating systems (OS), which comprise the environment that third-party developers – like Signal – build their apps to function and operate within. To put it differently, these three operating systems are the oceans in which Signal, and other applications, must swim; they dictate the conditions of life for the application ecosystem. Right now, these agentic AI integrations are changing this environment in a way that’s making it increasingly hostile to privacy. This is an existential threat to Signal, and our ability to responsibly uphold our mission.
In order to gain access to information about you, these OS AI agents “scan” the information that’s on your screen. In doing so, your Signal data is captured, then made available to these agentic systems in order to allow them to answer your questions and do your bidding.
The net result is that these AI capabilities in the operating system are undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy. For over a decade, this guarantee has been backed by our tried and trusted open source code base and our formally verified encryption protocol. These have been scrutinized by some of the best security experts and hackers across the world, and shown to be robust. Now, in service of AI agentic capabilities, your sensitive data is being captured, stored, and made accessible to whatever local database or remote server an OS-level AI agent is using at that moment. All of this is outside of Signal’s control once the data has been captured, and imperils the privacy of all the participants in a conversation.
So, we are blocking such capture by preventing screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and when AI assistants attempt to capture screen data on Android. 2
People who want the ability to take screenshots can disable this protection within the Signal app’s settings. However, doing so will potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees. Our remedy is also incomplete – while we are doing everything we can, restricting screenshots does not address other more sneaky ways AI agents could potentially access application data, such as retrieving content already present on a user’s device via the filesystem.
We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy. Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS. 3
We are also struggling with a significant lack of documentation about how these AI agents actually work. Over the past few months, we’ve spent considerable developer time and energy doing forensic investigations across Android and iOS in an attempt to learn what is actually happening when these AI systems access application data. Without better documentation and clear technical specifications, it will be increasingly difficult for Signal to provide robust privacy and security to the many millions of people who rely on us.
We continue to call on the major consumer operating system companies – Apple, Google, and Microsoft – to provide simple technical tools and accurate documentation that give developers like Signal ways to prevent AI agents from accessing sensitive application data. In particular, we are calling on these companies to provide two common-sense remedies that can protect the privacy so many millions of people rely on:
Developers should have an easy and well-documented way to opt their app out of AI data access and processing, including (but not limited to) screen reading, filesystem access, notifications, APIs, and other OS frameworks, all without undermining the core utility of an application.
Operating system companies should create better documentation and technical specifications around how these AI agents function, particularly regarding data access and processing. Confidential computing approaches are not a complete solution, and do not address these core concerns. In particular, these approaches still leave the power to determine the extent of privacy guarantees (if any) in the hands of these providers.
We also see a growing need for tools that can prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from accessing application data using the deep permissions that users are encouraged to grant them during setup. In many cases these agents are leveraging accessibility settings that were meant to empower actual people to get the most out of their apps and services, not to act as a skeleton key that provides access to AI agents.
In addition to taking these technical measures to block capture, we are engaging in conversations across

hn.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
hn.text:
All posts
We promoted developers into architects without informing them
Mani Doraisamy
30 minutes ago
0
0
Yesterday, I was debugging a performance problem with our Google Forms addon. It turned out my colleague had vibe coded the logging part, so that he could monitor the new installs every week. Monitoring new customers is the most important part of running a business, so he is absolutely right in doing that. Except, he was logging the user’s email and Google has severely restricted how much detail you can get about the user since last December. So, AI had written a series of try/catch statements:
First, try to get the email if the user gave consent to share it during installation.
If it fails, it would try to fetch his user ID.
If that fails, it would log an error saying the user has installed, but we don’t know his email or user ID.
All of these are one line of code, but internally each of these makes multiple API calls to Google servers. Since logging was the first line to execute after installation, the welcome screen took 15 seconds to load.
What is the right code for this?
If you are a senior developer or architect who understands the number of API calls behind each method, you would have:
Logged just the timestamp of the install instead of trying to fetch the email or user ID, and told the marketing team they won’t be able to send the follow-up email based on installation alone.
Or, if marketing wants the user’s email on install, you would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or user ID asynchronously from the browser, while the user is looking at the welcome screen. But calling your server from the addon’s welcome screen might require your server to bypass security and log an unauthenticated payload.
In other words, the job of the architect is to push back on requirements that can slow down performance. Or, find a way to work around the performance and security issues by making it async or accepting a reasonable compromise.
Why AI won’t push back
AI is great at writing code. But it doesn’t know if you are launching the app or have millions of users, which it needs to make the right architecture call to log a timestamp vs email. It is also sycophantic and tries to execute your requirements exactly without pushing back, which means you end up with a slow app that takes 15 seconds to load a static welcome screen.
Essentially, if you generate code by specifying your requirements instead of specifying your architecture, AI will decide the architecture on your behalf. It is so paranoid about security that it will never write code to accept an unauthenticated payload. Even if you write it yourself, it will rewrite it into an authenticated payload and screw up performance or force users to sign in again on your app.
Your new job is to architect
AI coding tools are tuned to implement your functional requirements and two non-functional requirements, i.e. security and backward compatibility to avoid breaking your app. This invariably leads to:
Architecture that trades off performance for security and slows down the app.
Multiple versions of datamodel design with redundant tables, columns and code.
That means you define the architecture, design the datamodel first and ask AI to code within that constraint. Every time you give a requirement that changes your architecture or design, coding tools have to ask you before changing it, instead of changing it on their own. You have to tell it when it needs to be backward compatible, so it’s ok to keep multiple versions of logic or database tables, and when to delete the old logic and tables and keep a single version for maintainability.
If you are an architect who is used to designing the datamodel, delegating the implementation to developers and then reviewing their code to see if they have implemented it correctly, this should be natural to you. But the problem is that today we have taken developers who were great at coding and moved them into an architect’s job. They see that the job they love, i.e. coding, is now completely done by AI. But nobody has told them about the new job of pushing back on requirements, designing the datamodel, constraining AI to their architecture and reviewing that it falls in line. This is the reason for all the confusion and hate among developers about vibe coding.
Your future as developer
In our case, the right fix is simple. Log the timestamp, show the welcome screen first and tell marketing what they can’t get on install. But AI will never make that call for you, because it doesn’t know your users and it won’t push back on your requirements. That is the architect’s job. If you are a developer, the coding job is going away. But it doesn’t mean your job is going away. Non-developers who don’t understand architecture and design will end up with bad performance and unmaintainable database tables. So, stop missing the coding and become an architect. Learn to push back on requirements, design the datamodel, constrain AI to it and review the code the way an architect reviews a developer’s code. You got promoted. Nobody told you, so I am telling you.

hn.title: Why YC Series A rounds fell off a cliff
hn.text:
Startup
Silicon Valley
Investing
Data Science
Venture Capital
On why YC Series A rounds fell off a cliff
Jared Heyman
4 min read ·
2 days ago
--
4
Listen
Share
As my long-time readers know, Rebel Fund invests in the top 10% of Y Combinator startups each batch, now with a portfolio of 300+ incredible YC companies. Because our Rebel Theorem 5.0 ML/AL algorithm tracks hundreds of characteristics and outcomes of every YC company and founder in history, we often see shifts in YC startup performance in our data well before they show up in the headlines.
We noticed one particular shift that set off alarm bells — YC startup Series A rounds fell off a cliff starting about 5 years ago:
Press enter or click to view image in full size
What happened? Did YC batches get too big? Is YC founder quality not what it used to be? Are macro factors at play? Today’s post sets out to answer this.
Why the Series A rate matters
Unsurprisingly, YC companies that raise a Series A have a dramatically higher survival rate than companies that don’t. According to our data, raising a Series A round cuts a company’s odds of shutting down by nearly 3x, and those that raise a Series C+ have a 10-year survival rate of >95%.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
Is YC not what it used to be?
There’s a perpetual meme amongst investors that “YC isn’t what it used to be”. I’ve been hearing this at every YC Demo Day since my own in 2013, but of course it’s no more true now than it was then.
If the 2021 and later batches were simply weaker, we’d expect to see two things in the data: 1) the slowdown would be confined to them, and 2) it would show up in our quality metrics of the founders and companies YC admitted. Neither turned out to be true.
Every batch slowed down in the same year
It turns out that Series A rounds slowed for every YC startup in 2023, regardless of whether they were admitted to YC one, two, or three plus years earlier. A drop in admissions quality around 2021 can’t reach back and slow down a company that went through YC in 2017.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
The founders were just as strong
At Rebel, we score every YC startup and founder across hundreds of dimensions using our proprietary Rebel Theorem 5.0 ML/AI model, looking at everything from founder education and work backgrounds, personality traits, archetypes , entrepreneurial track record, founder-product fit , and more.
For this analysis, we used the same data to predict overall Series A rates by batch, and compared that to actual graduation rates. In the chart below, you’ll see that predicted vs actual rates held steady until the end of 2020, and then suddenly the actual rates fell far below what our model predicted:
Press enter or click to view image in full size
The slowdown also hit every tier of founder quality about equally.
Press enter or click to view image in full size
To me, these are the most striking numbers in the whole analysis. A top-quintile founding team that went through YC in 2022 had worse odds of raising a Series A than a bottom-quintile team from 2018.
The market turned
The sudden slowdown in YC startup Series A rates coincides with interest rates climbing through 2022 and 2023. The pain started at the late stage, but global early-stage funding in late 2022 was down 39% year over year. As Series B and growth investors stopped writing checks, Series A investors lost confidence that their companies could raise the next round and stopped investing as aggressively.
It wasn’t just YC startups. Carta counted 808 Series A rounds in 2023, down about 50% from 1,612 the year before.
So there’s our answer: It was a macroeconomic phenomenon.
So what from here?
Many of the companies still standing from the tough 2021 time period onwards, which have founding teams just as strong as any before them, haven’t raised a Series A simply because the window was closed when they knocked.
However, there are early signs of a thaw. In 2025, the share of young YC companies raising a first Series A recovered to 4.2% for those one year past Demo Day and 7.3% for those two years past, up from 1.5% and 3.0% at the bottom. We’re still at roughly half the pre-2021 norm, so I wouldn’t call it a full recovery yet, but things are trending in the right direction.
The more interesting question is whether thanks to AI, companies will even need to raise a Series A at the same rates as before. In Rebel’s most recent vintages, we’re seeing incredible levels of revenue growth, capital efficiency, and profitability. If these companies can continue to fuel their growth on cash flow alone, they may not even want to raise any post-seed capital.
On the other hand, we’re also seeing companies take on dramatically more ambitious technological challenges than before, which could help maintain their appetite for venture capital after all, but that’s a topic for another blog post.

hn.title: PostgreSQL 19: A hands-on tour with runnable browser examples
hn.text:
A release you can try at the prompt
PostgreSQL 19 brings useful new SQL alongside maintenance and replication improvements. Try IGNORE NULLS , get-or-create inserts , JSON export , JSONPath transformations , and range subtraction , then explore planner advice and real replication.
PostgreSQL 19.0 · released 19 November 2026. The stable release announcement introduces the version installed in this sandbox. Each feature links to its official documentation. The release notes remain the complete change log.
About this terminal. Experiments run on a real PostgreSQL 19 server as student , in a disposable guest. Maintenance tables live in blog_lab . Replication experiments start additional real servers on demand: a logical subscriber on 5433 , and a physical standby on 5434 , both fed by the primary on 5432 . To fit the guest’s memory budget, only one of these extra instances runs at a time: each replication card stops the other and starts its own. Re-run that card before checking its current state again. Their first runs take longer because they initialize a cluster or take a base backup. Reset discards all three clusters and their data.
How to compare with 18. Sidenotes offer older SQL/workflows that you can run on 19, or a setting that disables a particular new optimization. These show the difference in expression or behavior. They do not turn PostgreSQL 19 into PostgreSQL 18. For timing claims, run the same workload on actual 18 and 19 servers with equal data, settings, cache conditions, and hardware.
Run the experiments in any order. Commands beginning with \! run a shell command from psql. The logical replication walkthrough shows its server setup and SQL directly; as-postgres runs server utilities as the Linux postgres account. Query and comparison examples state when to use another port or the administrative SQL role.
01 Start with the server you actually have
Before reading a release article, ask the server which release you are actually running. SELECT 1 is also a pleasantly boring connectivity test: a result beats a spinning status indicator.
The version returned below belongs to the sandbox , not to the release covered by the article. The SQL role is student ; ownership of the prepared demo database gives you room to experiment without administrative credentials.
Look for: one row, a real server version, and the expected role. Keep that baseline when you compare an upgrade later.
↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE Live SQL
From the shell, open the demo database ( PGDATABASE= blog_lab ):
psql ↗ RUN
Then run this at the SQL prompt:
SELECT 1 AS terminal_is_alive,
current_setting('server_version') AS actual_version,
current_user AS sql_role; ↗ RUN
Expected: One row with terminal_is_alive = 1, the installed server version, and student.
Run all steps ↗
02 REPACK — rewrite and reclaim space
Deleting rows leaves reusable space behind. Regular vacuum cleans that space; PostgreSQL 19’s native REPACK rewrites the table and returns unused bytes to the OS. The card deletes middle rows, preserving occupied tail pages so ordinary vacuum cannot simply truncate them. Compare the file size after vacuum with its size after a real rewrite. The tiny table demonstrates the operation, not a storage benchmark. REPACK documentation .
The concurrent variant uses logical decoding to capture intervening writes and takes an access-exclusive lock for the final swap. After the card, run this example at the same psql prompt. REPACK requires the table's MAINTAIN privilege; student owns events , so no role change is needed.
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY, ANALYZE) events;
Compare with 18: VACUUM (FULL, ANALYZE) events; performs the older blocking rewrite. For physical index ordering, compare CLUSTER events USING events_pkey; with REPACK events USING INDEX events_pkey; . Restore the same bloated table before each run. Use a second connection to try SELECT / INSERT while a larger rewrite runs, and inspect pg_locks : the concurrent form still locks briefly at the swap. PostgreSQL 18 has no native concurrent equivalent; the separately installed pg_repack extension is another workflow.
↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE Live SQL
DELETE FROM events WHERE id BETWEEN 301 AND 700; ↗ RUN
VACUUM (ANALYZE) events; ↗ RUN
SELECT pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_before_repack; ↗ RUN
REPACK (ANALYZE) events; ↗ RUN
SELECT count(*) AS surviving_events,
pg_relation_size('events') AS bytes_after_repack
FROM events
WHERE id <= 1000; ↗ RUN
Expected: DELETE 400 on the first run, VACUUM, REPACK, then 600 original surviving events. Compare bytes before/after; sizes vary.
Run all steps ↗
03 Autovacuum — inspect the real priority scores
Autovacuum now prioritizes tables using real scores and can parallelize index work. The card reads pg_stat_autovacuum_scores and the configured score weights. Use \x on to show the wide scores view as readable records, then \x off to return to a table for the two-column settings query. Scores change with workload and statistics, so zero after maintenance is a useful result too. Autovacuum scheduling , statistics views .
autovacuum_max_parallel_workers controls the server-wide allowance; autovacuum_parallel_workers is a per-table setting. The sandbox’s current parallel allowance is zero, so the card inspects priorities rather than launching parallel vacuum work. PostgreSQL 19 can also mark eligible pages all-visible during ordinary scans, improving future index-only scans.
Compare with 18: On an administrative connection, set autovacuum_max_parallel_workers = 0 with ALTER SYSTEM , then reload using SELECT pg_reload_conf(); to disable this new parallel index work. Restore the previous value afterward. Manual VACUUM (PARALLEL 0) versus VACUUM (PARALLEL 2) is also runnable on 18, but measures manual vacuum. There is no faithful switch back to PostgreSQL 18’s autovacuum scheduler; compare the scheduling on separate installations.
↳ TRY IT / CURRENT IMAGE Live SQL
\x on ↗ RUN
SELECT *
FROM pg_stat_autovacuum_scores
WHERE relid IN ('events'::r

hn.title: Google Workers Tell Their Employer Not to Punish Schools That Don't Want AI
hn.text:
Chromebooks are distributed to students through a fence at a Los Angeles Unified School District high school for during the Covid quarantine. Sarah Reingewirtz/MediaNews Group/Pasadena Star-News/Getty
Get your news from a source that’s not owned and controlled by oligarchs. Sign up for the free Mother Jones Daily .
Hundreds of workers at Google are pushing senior leadership to retract a policy that would block schools who turn off its Gemini AI tools from access to the company’s search engine starting next year.
Google made the surprise announcement two weeks ago, on Election Day, with executives saying they wanted to address teachers and parents’ concerns around AI in the classroom. Since then, communities across the country have protested Google’s tight hold on tech in many schools.
As I wrote last week after attending a rally in New York City:
Attendees of all ages held signs reading, “NO AI IN MY SCHOOL!”, “A.I. Gets an F,” “Stop stealing our imaginations,” and “SCHOOL Librarians = THE BEST Search Engines.” Some students handed out fliers to passersby while younger children ran around and drew pictures off to the side.
Many cars driving by honked their horns in support, and a few construction workers on the other side of the one-way street cheered the protesters on.
That day, protests took place in six other cities —Los Angeles; Chicago; Boston; Portland, Oregon; Boulder, Colorado; and Durham, North Carolina—all organized by a nationwide alliance of parent and community advocacy organizations.
School districts across the country use the company’s software and Chromebooks , which were more affordable than Windows and Apple computers when many were quickly assembling remote learning programs during the early years of the Covid pandemic. The Chromebooks have built-in AI classroom tools, and Google Search embeds AI Overview and AI Mode powered by Gemini.
Responding to the backlash, three of the largest school districts in the US—New York City, Los Angeles, and Chicago—are now discussing alternative search engines.
“Any opportunity to drive positive change with AI in education will rely on educators having the freedom to choose how to implement it in their curriculum,” employees wrote in a petition brought by the Alphabet Workers Union , which represents more than 1,000 workers at Google’s parent company. “Cutting off access to Search for schools that don’t wish to use AI will not help persuade our users, and will more likely result in them shutting out Google products altogether.”
“It is our job as Googlers to respect the user, and listen to them when they have concerns about our products,” they continued, addressing Alphabet and Google CEO Sundar Pichai, Google vice president and general manager of education Chris Phillips, and Elizabeth Reid, its vice president and head of search.
A software engineer in Google’s education department told me on Thursday that most workers did not know about the Google Search decision before it was publicly announced. Corporate leadership has now acknowledged the letter but has not responded to any of its specific demands.
AI classroom tools should be “built responsibly and prioritize the best interests of the students, not the company’s bottom line,” the Google engineer said.
Another engineer and union member in New York, who also signed the petition, said to Mother Jones that the executive team “seems convinced that resistance to AI adoption is because people don’t see the vision.”
That goes beyond teachers, parents, and students: the Google staffer said their colleagues are also concerned about how the company is implementing their work on AI tools.
“If the tech is really as useful and desirable as they think it is, why don’t they trust us to choose to use it on our own terms?” the engineer asked.
Google has been contacted for comment.

hn.title: Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
hn.text:
Internet Policy
Why there are still no non-WebKit browsers on iOS
November 20, 2026
Mozilla
Firefox on iPhone is growing fast across the world. This is especially true in the EU since 2024, when the EU Digital Markets Act (DMA) started requiring Apple to let people choose their default browser; millions have picked Firefox, and daily use on iOS has doubled. People want to choose the browser on their phone.
But there remains an important limitation to what is available on iPhones: Apple forces all browsers on iOS to be built on Apple’s own browser engine.
This has meant that companies like Mozilla cannot easily bring the full range of Firefox features and functionality to iPhone users because many of these are built within our browser engine , Gecko. iPhones and iPads are unique in having this restriction. On all other major operating systems, including Apple’s macOS, people can access the Gecko-powered version of Firefox.
As a result of the DMA, Apple began allowing alternative browser engines on iOS in the EU. It published a set of conditions that companies like Mozilla must comply with to bring their own browser engine. At the time we said Apple’s rules made it “as painful as possible” for alternatives like Gecko. In the meantime, Japan also introduced new rules requiring alternative browser engines on iOS. Apple applied very similar conditions in Japan to those in the EU.
Nearly three years since Apple introduced these conditions in the EU and almost a year since Japan, not one developer has been able to launch a non-WebKit browser on iOS. The reason is simple: Apple’s conditions remain unworkable. The real test of any rule is whether it delivers the change it was meant to achieve in practice. Compliance on paper alone falls short of that test.
Since the DMA came into effect we’ve been working behind the scenes to test and improve Apple’s conditions so that we can bring Gecko to iOS users. Those efforts have so far largely failed.
One of the conditions requires us not to disclose non-public information related to the project, but here’s an example of what we are up against: to use Gecko, we can’t simply update the Firefox app people already use and love. We’d have to build a whole separate app, a second Firefox. Then we’d have to ask every Firefox user to download it, move their bookmarks, passwords and history across, and manually switch over, step by confusing step.
That’s a lot to ask of people who already made their choice. A significant proportion of people would understandably give up, including many who picked Firefox from the EU’s choice screen.
The conditions Apple imposes, including a level of user friction Apple would never accept for its own apps, mean that the open door feels more like a trap door.
Firefox users on iPhone chose an independent browser. They should get everything that comes with it, including Gecko, the last major browser engine not developed by a big tech company. We’ll keep pushing for a real level playing field, not an opening that drops independent browsers through the floor.

microSD card expanding the amount of photos you can take on the move.

hn.title: The G1 Garbage Collector
hn.text:
The G1 Garbage Collector
Introduction
The Garbage-First Garbage Collector (G1) is the default garbage collector on the JVM as of JDK 27, with JEP 523: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector in All Environments , which made it the default in all environments. It had been the default garbage collector in "server" environments since JDK 9, with JEP 248: Make G1 the Default Garbage Collector . G1 seeks to balance throughput and latency and is a good option for many workloads. In this article, we will cover a brief history of G1, its key design concepts, and how to use it.
A Brief History of G1
G1 was originally introduced in JDK 6u14 as an experimental feature, promoted to a standard feature in JDK 7u4, and designated the default garbage collector in JDK 9, taking over that role from ParallelGC. While G1 has taken over the role of default garbage collector from Parallel, it was originally introduced to replace the CMS (Concurrent-Mark-Sweep) Garbage Collector, which was deprecated in JDK 9 and removed in JDK 14.
At the time of its introduction, G1 was designed for server environments. Systems using G1 were expected to have multiple processors and large amounts of system memory (tens of GB) available. Continued development of G1 has reduced its system requirements, and now G1 can provide good performance even in resource constrained environments with only a single CPU and less than 2 GB of available system memory. This is why, as of JDK 27, it is the default garbage collector across all system configurations.
In garbage collector design, the three primary design constraints are throughput, latency (pause time), and memory footprint. G1 seeks to maintain a balance between latency and throughput, rather than heavily optimizing for either. By comparison, ParallelGC primarily focuses on maximizing throughput, and ZGC focuses on minimizing latency. G1 also aims for more consistent pause times than the CMS collector it replaced.
As of the writing of this article, 12 JEPs relating to G1 have been delivered since JDK 8, with more changes planned for the future. Continued development has steadily improved G1's throughput, latency, and memory footprint.
G1 Design and Collection Cycle
G1 is a generational, incremental, parallel, mostly concurrent, stop-the-world, and evacuating garbage collector. For an explanation of each of these terms, check the Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors article on dev.java. This section covers some of the key design characteristics of G1.
As mentioned in the previous section, G1 was originally designed with large "server-like" environments in mind. G1 is capable of efficiently marshalling the resources of systems with dozens of cores and addressing heaps measured in tens of GB.
G1 Heap Layout
Figure 03-01: Simplified representation of the G1 heap layout
G1 divides the heap into a set of regions (increments) of uniform size. Figure 03-01 is a simplified example of what the G1 heap space would look like. The size and number of regions, unless otherwise configured, are based on internal heuristics, with the overall heap size being the primary influence on both. These regions are then divided up into eden, survivor, old, and humongous regions.
Eden and survivor regions are both part of the "young" generation. On creation, an object is placed in an eden region. If that object survives a collection, it is evacuated (copied) into a survivor region. Unreachable objects are not deleted individually; rather, the region they are a part of is considered empty and is eligible for reuse by G1. Surviving objects, if they remain reachable, will be evacuated to a new survivor region on subsequent collections. If an object survives enough collections, based on internal heuristics unless otherwise configured, it will be evacuated to an old region, which is checked less frequently.
A humongous region is a contiguous space of one or more regions, reserved for a single "humongous" object. An object qualifies as "humongous" if it's larger than half the size of a single region. Humongous objects bypass the eden and survivor regions and are treated as equivalent to an old region by G1.
G1 Garbage Collection Cycle
Figure 03-02: Simplified representation of the G1 garbage collection cycle
The G1 garbage collection cycle (GC cycle) consists of both stop-the-world and concurrent behavior, both of which can run in parallel. Again, check Garbage Collection Concepts and JVM Collectors for definitions of these terms. Figure 03-02 is a simplified visualization of the G1 GC cycle and will help to contextualize this section.
At a high level, the G1 GC cycle consists of two phases: Young-Only and Space-Reclamation. G1 will start in the Young-Only phase, which, as the name suggests, means only young regions are collected. In G1, when a collection happens, the application is paused while G1 evacuates objects to new regions or performs other GC work.
The concurrent behavior of G1 is primarily concerned with determining which objects in old regions are still active. The concurrent phase can be broken into three distinct parts and starts when old-generation occupancy reaches a threshold.
Concurrent Start is the first step in the concurrent phase and is a special pause. During this pause, normal evacuation of young regions still occurs, and G1 also initiates concurrent marking of old-generation regions to determine which objects are still reachable. It is also possible that G1 determines there is no need to follow through with marking, in which case a Concurrent Mark Undo pause occurs, and the Young-Only phase continues.
Remark is the second step in the concurrent phase. This is a special pause where no evacuation of young regions happens. Instead, during this pause, G1 finalizes concurrent marking and performs other work, such as reference processing, class unloading, and reclaiming empty regions. Between this phase and Cleanup, G1 will concurrently calculate information to be used during the Space-Recla
