hn.text:
Access All Areas / By Mark Gidley
The Making of Oxygene
The full story of the ground-breaking Oxygene album and how it has been re-imagined for Dolby Atmos
Chapters
5
Interviews
1
Read
01 Oxygene - The History Chapters
01 / Feature
Oxygene - The History
In late 1976, an album was released which re-wrote the rulebook of synthesizers and electronic music and captured the hearts and imagination of the entire world. Composed by the then unknown 28-year-old French artist Jean-Michel Jarre, the album Oxygène broke out of France to become a top 10 album in seven different countries, spending a remarkable 24 weeks in the UK album charts and selling now close to 20 million copies worldwide.
Uniquely, the album consisted of just six tracks, numbered Oxygène Parts 1 through 6, and was entirely instrumental with no acoustic instruments whatsoever, which was unheard of in 1976.
Jean Michel Jarre tells the story of the making of his ground-breaking album in his own words.
"Around 1969, I felt that the world of classical music, the world of rock and other forms of music were a bit narrow and living in their own worlds. I had the feeling it was the right time to explore other fields to perhaps see if a combination of different styles were possible.
“The main difference with electronic music is that you create music in terms of sound, not just notes. It’s something else entirely. When I was a teenager, I always liked processing my guitar or organ or whatever, playing the tape backwards and changing the speed. Then the drummer in my band said, ‘You should meet with these crazy guys at Groupe De Recherches Musicales [GRM] in Paris who are working in French public radio. They’re doing the same kinds of things as you, and they have labs.’
“When I first went there, I was immediately seduced by what they were doing. Electronic music owes a lot to public radio stations - the BBC Radiophonic Workshop, the German lab where Stockhausen was working and, of course, the one in Paris.
"Pierre Schaeffer was one of the most brilliant guys of the century in terms of what he brought to the music world. He created the notion of Musique concrète and influenced me a lot in this direction. Saying that, I felt that contemporary music had got a very elitist attitude - a bit too intellectual vis-à-vis the music and it created barriers between the audience and yourself. I wanted to be much more open to the audience.
"I stayed with Pierre Schaeffer [and Pierre Henry] for three years and I also went to Cologne to work with Stockhausen. He was totally crazy, but a real genius. He considered himself to be made of sound, biologically, so he had a kind of surrealistic approach. Crazy, but realistic at the same time. It was very interesting.
"When I left GRM and through to 1976, I did production work for some rock artists, earning enough to set up a studio in my kitchen. I didn’t have much equipment, though, just a few guitar pedals and my first synthesizer, the VCS3, which looked like a telephone exchange. I realised that using a Revox tape machine to delay the sound that came out of one loudspeaker created a huge sense of space.
“The British-made VCS3 from EMS [Electronic Music Studios, based in London] was created by a genius called Peter Zinovieff. It was a kind of poor European version of the Moog. In those days Europe was not as rich as the States, so the sound was drier. In a sense, it was a kind of punk synthesizer - there was something very harsh and rough about it. I loved it; I still take one on stage with me today.
“At the time, I was obsessed with this idea of creating a bridge between experimentation and pop melody. I liked this kind of challenge, playing around with sound design and integrating melodies. Oxygène was a new start for music with analogue synthesizers"
The album was recorded on a Scully recorder with just eight tracks, and all through a home-made mixer. On top of the VCS3, Jarre had managed to add some other classic equipment including EMS Synthi AKS and ARP 2600 synths, an Eminent String Ensemble, an RMI Harmonic Synthesizer, and Farfisa organ, while an RMI Keyboard Computer was used for some sequencing.
Jarre continues, “I really did it in a kind of home way using what, I think, was one of the first home studios. I had just three or four synthesizers and was using a Scully eight–track and a mixture of Ampex 256 and 3M tape. The whole album was done on just one eight–track and you can hear that in the piece — it’s quite minimalist and I think that contributes to its timelessness.
“Nothing is repeated the same way. Each sound, even if appears to be the same, has a slightly different attack and release, and, as the sequences are being made by hand, by definition they are not the same. Even the sounds of the drum machines were filtered in a very subtle way to give life inside the patterns.
”Michel Geiss was a maintenance technician, at a famous French record company at that time called Barclay and I met him because he was very interested in electronic instruments. He visited my home and we started to experiment. He was teaching me to use the first semi-modular synths I could put my hands on. And then step by step we worked together, Michel mainly as a kind of sound engineer for me.
“For Oxygene, he was working at his record company as a maintenance guy during the day, and he was coming to work with me at night. In those days I probably had the first home studio in France, when the serious music was done in serious recording studios with a window where God was the sound engineer behind the window, and we were just on the other side as musicians. For electronic music you need to match the mixing area with the main studio to record your own sounds.
“So, I had this home studio in a kitchen in the flat I had in Paris, and Michel joined me, using one of the first eight-track tape recorders to record my music. I only had two tapes. So, I had no choice if I was not happy with something to erase what I'd done the previo

hn.title: Lovable: Now you can explore any idea in parallel without touching what's live
hn.text:
The best builders experiment, tinker, and tweak. Now you and your team can try different ideas in parallel and see how they'd really look in the wild before choosing your favorite, while your live app stays untouched.
With drafts, you can copy your whole app, from design to database, as often as you like. Each draft has its own chat and preview, so you and your team can work on separate versions and compare them side by side. Nothing goes live until you accept a draft and hit publish.
Here's what that means for you:
Bring your people in without losing control
Let a teammate or a client make changes in their own draft without altering the existing app. Review each draft and choose which changes to keep.
Our sales teams have been building their own tools with Lovable, from the Sales hub where we manage our sales pipeline to our demo library. Drafts let us try a few ideas at once and see how each one actually works with real-looking data, without risking the progress we've made or interrupting work in another part of the app.
Jeremy Maher , Director Sales Engineering, Observe.AI
Explore multiple ideas at once
Try out different ideas and keep what works. Every draft comes filled with example data, so instead of an empty page you see your idea with a busy booking calendar, a full order history, or a long list of sign-ups. You can even ask Lovable to spin up different versions for you and keep the ones you like.
Make changes safely
Build and test changes on a full copy of your app, including its own backend when needed, before putting them in front of real customers. Try a new field on your sign-up form or a members-only page, without test entries landing next to real customer data.
OLX runs online marketplaces across 7+ countries. We use drafts to test different features, layouts and UX side by side, then keep what works best. We can explore as much as we want without worrying about what's already live.
Shane Stuart , Director of Product Design & Research, OLX Global
Examples of what you can do
Now that each draft is a full copy of your app, backend included when needed, you can easily explore any new idea for your app, for example:
A new field on your sign-up or booking form
Who can see what, like a members-only page or an admin view
A new dashboard, seen with months of example data
New tables and records, without test entries landing next to real user data
Deposits, a waitlist, or a new booking flow, visualized with a full example calendar
Fresh layouts, images, videos, and sharper copy
How it works
Open a project, click its name at the top of the editor, and hit "New draft." Lovable creates a complete copy of your app, from design to database. To edit the draft, just start prompting. You can create as many drafts as you like.
When you're happy with a draft, hit accept to add its changes to your project, then hit publish to make them live. Any data you add while testing stays in the draft and is cleared when you accept or delete it, so it never lands next to real customer data.
Changed your mind? Before you accept, just delete the draft. After you accept, you can still roll it back before you publish: open History, pick the version from before you accepted, and hit revert.
Try drafts now

hn.text:

03:17

By Rob Wile
A bruising stock market sell-off gathered steam Friday, despite high hopes that Anthropic’s record-setting IPO a day earlier would revive sentiment around the flagging AI trade.
Instead, Friday’s downturn was led by Anthropic itself, whose shares were down more than 11% after rising 17% on its first day on the Nasdaq Composite.
The S&P 500 was trading nearly 2% lower as it headed for its worst losing week since April 2025, when President Donald Trump announced his “Liberation Day” tariffs, and is now 10% off from its most recent high, entering what’s known as “correction territory.”
Meanwhile, the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was off more than 3% and officially erasing all its previous gains in 2026. Other major AI-related names such as CoreWeave, Nvidia and Oracle also sold off.
The six consecutive declining S&P 500 sessions mark the index’s longest losing streak since April 2024. A seventh losing day would make it the longest stretch since the pandemic slump in February 2020, according to Deutsche Bank.
For U.S. households relying on 401(k)s and pension funds for retirement, the downturn is especially unwelcome at a time when inflation continues to prove stubborn.
Samyukta Lakshmi / Bloomberg via Getty Given the importance the AI trade has played this year in propelling markets and economic growth writ large, its derailment over concerns about costs, debt, profitability and political risk could have broader implications.
Deepening worries about AI revenues tied to exports of advanced technology to China compounded Friday’s sell-off.

hn.title: Show HN: Fast deterministic natural language search for OpenStreetMap data
hn.text: I want to show you HippoMaps. It is a fully featured map and navigation app built on OpenStreetMap with a custom Overpass API engine for really fast search of POIs, areas and ways. My aim with HippoMaps is to get to a level where I don't need Google Maps anymore. The biggest hurdle IMHO with OSM based apps is the lack of nice and fast search (where GMaps excels at). To get there I started working on a deterministic (as in no LLMs used) parser of queries that translates them to the Overpass QL. Search queries are split into tokens and the algorithm tries to guess "what" you want to search and "where". The former comes from a word list (known brands, sports, OSM tags) and the latter from the geocoder service (Photon). You can get quite creative like "cafes in Zurich by the Limmat", "peaks over 4000 m in Valais", "pharmacies open now in Bern". It's good for discovering hiking trails, e.g. "hiking trails from Arth-Goldau to Rigi Kulm". It knows how to find stuff between two places, next to a place, near a place and so on. You can stack those as well like "bridges over the danube in serbia 50 km from novi sad". Except the search it has almost all of the features you would expect from a map like turn-by-turn navigation (Valhalla) with voice (Piper), public transport navigation in Europe (MOTIS), live traffic (only a few countries so far). The app is GPL-3.0: https://github.com/cdutsov/hippomaps I'm looking forward to feedback on searches that work or don't work for you + overall comments.

Copy link
Copy Markdown

This fixes "Buffer overflow in EVP_EncodeBlock()" ( CVE-2026-121481 ) by returning -1 for invalid inputs to EVP_EncodeBlock() : NULL input or output buffers, negative lengths, and lengths for which the encoded size does not fit in an int . The OpenSSL SRT has asked for it to be fixed publicly; the advisory is still pending.
Returning -1 for invalid inputs is the most straightforward fix, and matches what happens in wolfSSL's compatibility layer for OpenSSL's EVP_EncodeBlock() .
I'm suggesting a similar guard for EVP_DecodeBlock() . No length limit is needed here because the decoded length always fits in an int , but it is a good idea to reject NULL buffers and negative lengths.
Moreover, I propose to fix the incorrect length check in the base64encode() function of http_client.c , which rejected only len > INT_MAX .
I am adding tests in test/base64_dec_avx2_test.c to cover the new behavior, and documenting the -1 returns in doc/man3/EVP_EncodeInit.pod .
Exploiting this vulnerability from the command line is possible by passing a large -proxy_pass to openssl s_client . I confirmed that GOST accepts these large passwords out of the box. However, the password has to be supplied through an environment variable ( env:VAR ), otherwise the command line will be too long.
Note: the pattern of CVE-2026-121481 is similar to that of CVE-2021-23840 .

Hi Tomas,

Both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() can legitimately return 0, so 0 is not an error for either function. EVP_EncodeBlock() returns 0 when dlen == 0, and EVP_DecodeBlock() returns 0 when the input is empty after trimming.
Also, for EVP_DecodeBlock(), the current failure paths (e.g., trimmed length not a multiple of invalid base64 characters) all return -1. So, I wanted to make sure that both EVP_EncodeBlock() and EVP_DecodeBlock() consistently return -1 on any error. As I mentioned before, returning -1 is also what WolfSSL does in its OpenSSL compatibility layer.
I understand the concern that third-party callers may cast the return to size_t without checking. But are we not making things more difficult for third-party calls if both 0 and -1 can indicate errors, or if the existing EVP_DecodeBlock() errors will be changed from -1 to 0?

hn.title: If you stop writing code, you also get worse at reviewing it
hn.text:
Whatever skill you’re learning, it won’t take long before someone with experience in that particular field tells you to get your hands dirty. It’s fine to read “Born to Run”, but you won’t be running an ultra marathon any time soon if you don’t start running. Whether it’s muscle memory, technique, physical fitness or problem solving you need to work on to reach your goals, you need to practice . This isn’t a controversial statement in any field at all , and has never really been.
Except in software engineering, somehow.
When it comes to software engineering, we somehow lost our way, thinking that our skills won’t stop improving if we stop practicing . Making such a claim in any other field would be sneered at at best. Imagine John Scofield 1 saying he stopped practicing his guitar because “he was at a good enough level, musically, to maintain (and even improve!) his expertise” simply by 1) instructing others on how to play (either in vibe general terms, or with a strict spec musical notation), and then 2) listening to what they played and iterating until it sounded good enough for his next record. “My music is better”, he would claim, and moreover “actually playing the guitar was never the point anyway, there’s more to making music.”
Mind you, my point in this post is not to discuss the short term quality of code output (or recorded guitar playing, to continue the proverbial thread), but rather the skill of the craftsman practicing his craft vs the one who doesn’t practice at all.
To make another comparison that’s arguably closer to software engineering, or at least the “writing and reasoning about code” part of it, let’s look at authors in other fields. I have no doubt that reading great prose has the potential to nudge a writer towards better writing of his/her own; in fact it’s super important to have creative references to draw upon - no doubt at all. But, imagine an author who 1) stopped writing, and only pursued reading and giving feedback to other writers, and worse yet 2) mostly read AI generated prose !? To be perfectly honest, I would expect a quite steady (if not exponential) decline of this author’s writing skills.
“There’s more to software engineering than writing code”
Link to heading
Sure. But if we can at least agree that the code that runs our software is a non-trivial part of it (though, granted, not all of it by far: The other parts of developing and maintaining software speak even louder against using generative AI as a significant tool service! ), we should aspire to be proficient in understanding how code works, what good code looks like, what to watch out for and how software architecture plays a vital part in making code Easy To Change.
Simply “reviewing all the code Claude produced” won’t quite cut it. And who are you trying to fool, after all; at this point you’re not really reading half of it, are you?
So I propose something that used to be a no-brainer: Keep practicing!
Which brings me to my next point:
All engineers(!) need to be good at solving problems
Link to heading
if || while you can argue that the need for being hands-on on your software’s code varies, I propose you can’t argue that we’re still solving problems . And the moment you stop practicing solving problems is the moment you stop getting better at it, just like everything else. Simple as that. This is hardly new, btw: you could always tell who beat Doom using cheat codes and who finished the game the real way! If the end goal is to “beat the game”, then by all means cheat; if the end goal is getting good at it , then I’d advice you not to. Some lessons are only learned the hard way (trial and error ), and very few are learned without effort at all . Repeated LLM usage for problem solving pounds the following premise into our brain’s wiring: If something is hard, tricky or requires effort, you shouldn’t even try. And right there goes our learning, craft and joy, right out the window.
In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don’t want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can’t help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea .
It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?
— Em’s blog 2 , emphasis mine.
Please, John Scofield, don’t stop playing your guitar!
↩︎
I’m not sure who Em is, but their blog is great! ↩︎

hn.title: Carnival Cruises emits ten times more sulphur oxide than all of Europe's cars (2019)
hn.text:
In April, Ecohustler disrupted Carnival Cruise's AGM calling on the shareholders to reduce their company's pollution using straight forward and affordable methods - like burning cleaner fuel. Since then, a new report outlines the corporation's impact on the coastline of Europe. These vast floating cities are burning dirty bunker fuel and creating shocking levels of air pollution wherever they go. Shipping has been an unregulated industry for too long and action is urgently required.
Carnival Corporation, the world’s largest luxury cruise operator, emitted nearly 10 times more sulphur oxide (SOx) around European coasts than did all 260 million European cars in 2017, a new analysis by sustainable transport group Transport & Environment reveals.
Royal Caribbean Cruises, the world’s second largest, is second, yet four times worse than the European car fleet. SOx emissions form sulphate (SO4) aerosols that increase human health risks and contribute to acidification in terrestrial and aquatic environments.
SUPPORTED BY HEROES LIKE YOU
Support independent eco journalism that drives real change.
JOIN US →
In absolute terms, Spain, Italy and Greece, closely followed by France and Norway, are the European countries most exposed to SOx air pollution from cruise vessels while Barcelona, Palma de Mallorca and Venice are the most impacted European port cities, followed by Civitavecchia (Rome) and Southampton.
All photos by Greg English ©
These countries are so exposed because they are major tourist destinations, but also because they have less stringent marine sulphur fuel standards which allows cruise ships to burn the dirtiest most sulphurous fuel all along their coastlines.
Faig Abbasov, shipping policy manager at T&E, said: “Luxury cruise ships are floating cities powered by some of the dirtiest fuel possible. Cities are rightly banning dirty diesel cars but they’re giving a free pass to cruise companies that spew out toxic fumes that do immeasurable harm both to those on board and on nearby shores. This is unacceptable.“
NOX emissions from cruise ships in Europe also heavily impact some cities, equivalent to about 15% of the nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted by Europe’s passenger car fleet in a year, the report finds. In Marseille, for example, 57 cruise ships emitted in 2017 almost as much NOx as one-quarter of the city’s 340,000 passenger cars. Along the coasts of countries such as Norway, Denmark, Greece, Croatia and Malta a handful of cruise ships are also responsible for more NOx than the majority of their domestic car fleet.
Europe should implement a zero-emission port standard as soon as possible, this could then be extended to other ship types. The report also recommends extending emission control areas (ECAs), currently in place only in the North and Baltic Seas and English Channel, to the rest of the European seas. Furthermore, the report recommends regulating NOx emissions from existing ships, which are currently exempt from NOx standards applying in emission control areas.
Faig Abbasov concluded “There are enough mature technologies to clean up cruise ships. Shore-side electricity can help cut in-port emissions, batteries are a solution for shorter distances and hydrogen technology can power even the biggest cruise ships. The cruise sector are apparently not willing to make the shift voluntarily, so we need governments to step in and mandate zero emission standards.”

hn.title: µ-Wire – USB on an ATtiny 10
hn.text:
Atmels AVR ATtiny10 are surprisingly powerful devices that come in an extremely tiny SOT23 package with only 6 pins. The have 1kb of flash, 32 bytes of SRAM and use the reduced AVR core which only supports 16 instead of 32 register. It seems like Atmels idea of these devices is to use them as an advanced blinker , and to replace tiny logic circuits. But other people have shown that much more is possible. For example the noiseplug (video) , a chiptune player, and a Simon Says game .
I previously used the ATtiny10 in the TinyTouchbutton , a touchbutton controlled light with WS2812 LEDs. This time I aimed higher: Is it possible to turn the ATtiny10 into a USB compatible device? My goal was to implement a subset of the little-wire functionality to control a WS2812 LED by USB. This takes 3 I/O lines, which is exactly the number of free pins on the ATtiny10.
Littlewire supports several functions to control WS2812 LEDs on arbitrary I/O ports. I simplified this to only supporting a single LED on a specific pin, however still retained protocol compatibility. This means that all the little-wire host-programs still work. The finished device can, for example, be used as an RGB indicator LED similar to the Blink(1).
My test setup is shown below. The ATtiny10 is almost the smallest part of the circuit. There are some discrete components on the rear-side of all PCBs, so do not be surprised about missing decoupling capacitors, zener diodes and resistors.
Implementation
The V-USB USB interface requires more than 1.5kb of flash in its smallest implementation and uses more than 50 bytes of ram, including stack usage. Additional code is required to implement the littlewire interface and to write to the WS2812. The ATtiny10 has 1kb of flash, 32 bytes of SRAM and only 16 instead of 32 registers. So this ended up as a nice exercise in cutting down V-USB to its bare essentials – and further.
A main step towards reducing the memory footprint was to switch to an interrupt-free implementation of V-USB , as developed for micronucleus . This allowed to reduce the SRAM footprint by omitting register saving on the stack and avoiding double buffering. In turn, this also allowed reducing the program size. The image below shows a timing diagram of an incoming USB packet, instructing to set the LED color, and the access to the WS2812 LED. The controller “steals” the time to write out to the WS2812 by ignoring the following USB data packet and catching up after the host resends it. This strict in-order processing allows to avoid the need of moving the data around in memory.
AVR-GCC issues
One major annoyance during this project was AVR-GCC. Even though I used the newest versions of Atmels toolchain (4.8.1), the ATtiny10 support is still quite buggy. The ATtiny 4/5/9/10 come with a “reduced” AVR CPU core. One change is the introduction of different memory access instructions. Instead of 2 word LDS/STS, a 1 word LDS/STS is supported, which allows single cycle access to the SRAM. Unfortunately, AVR-GCC simply does not generate these instructions. Instead, indirect memory access via the Z-Register is used.
What I want:
uint8_t value0 = rq->wValue.bytes[0];
lds r22,0x54
What I get:
uint8_t value0 = rq->wValue.bytes[0];
344: e4 e5 ldi r30, 0x54 ; 84
346: f0 e0 ldi r31, 0x00 ; 0
348: 60 81 ld r22, Z
AVR-GCC effectively wastes 4 bytes for every variable access. I submitted a support ticket to Atmel around 3 months ago, but this seems to be a low priority issue to them. A pity they do not value support of their smallest microcontrollers higher, but maybe people are really only using them for very low complexity tasks.
I worked around this issue by using defines (see also this thread ).
#define STS(mem,in) \
asm volatile ("sts %0,%1" : : "i" (&mem), "r" (in) : "memory" );
#define LDS(out,mem) \
asm volatile ("lds %0,%1" : "=d" (out) : "i" (&mem));
Example:
uint8_t value0 = rq->wValue.bytes[0]; // 6 bytes
uint8_t value0; LDS(value0,rq->wValue.bytes[0]); // 2 bytes
Further measures to reduce code size:
I clocked the controller at 12 MHz using the internal RC oscillator and calibrated from the USB bus timing. The 12 MHz V-USB implementation is much smaller than the recommended 12.8 MHz version, but it does not come with an internal phase locked loop to cope with the more inaccurate RC-oscillator timing. Surprisingly I did not observe any timing errors.
Since the reduced core AVR only support 16 registers, I had to manually remap numerous registers in V-USB to avoid collisions with GCC.
I removed all handling of the reset signal on the USB-Bus. This means the device will not properly re-enumerate when a bus reset is issued. But this is not a problem if you plug it in after the PC was turned on.
V-USB was completely gutted and integrated into the main loop. It only support SETUP requests to a single endpoint now. All additional functions have been removed. This also reduces stack usage as fewer subroutine calls are required.
I removed the code to support replies from the SRAM. Data can only be sent from flash. This is possible since only single byte-replies are required to implement the protocol, apart from the fixed USB configuration replies which are stored in the flash.
Final Stats
Flash: 988 of 1024 bytes used (96.4%)
SRAM: 28 (variables)+2 (stack) of 32 bytes used (93.8%)
This is most likely the most complex firmware ever loaded into an ATtiny10!
You can find all the code in the Github repository.
Bonus
Bonus below, it also works with the new 8mm WS2812 LEDs .

Postgres 19 REPACK: Faster, Built-In Table Bloat Cleanup
Craig Kerstiens
REPACK is my favorite feature in Postgres 19. It's not the flashiest, but it is the one that’s going to matter most if you’re running a production database. Vacuum, autovacuum and bloat have always been this sore spot for Postgres users. On the one hand, Postgres MVCC design is not new. And yet, on high update systems, this churn of having dead rows that get freed up later, vacuum being tweaked to the right levels to maintain low bloat is still a bit of an inexact science.
Once bloat does exist, it’s just sitting there. And you see that unclaimed space not being used.
Before Postgres 19, your options for reclaiming that space were:
VACUUM FULL: Built-in, but takes a read/write lock for the entire duration. On a large table, that means minutes of downtime.
dump/restore : Fail over to a fresh database that is a clean snapshot.
pg_repack: A third-party extension for online rebuilds from an external process. Generally a good option, but not without caveats and risks.
pg_squeeze: Another third-party extension for online rebuilds via a background worker, also solid in production but again not without caveats and risks.
Enter Postgres 19:
REPACK CONCURRENTLY : reclaims bloated table space while the table stays fully readable and writable, takes only a brief lock at the very end, and runs without any extension
How Postgres tables become bloated
Let’s back up. You may be familiar with bloat as a seasoned Postgres user, but just to make sure we’re all on the same page… It's one of those Postgres realities, the tradeoff for MVCC. Tables accumulate dead tuples over time: when rows are updated or deleted, the old versions stick around. Regular autovacuum typically marks that space as reusable. For most tables, that's enough. But for large, update-intensive tables, vacuum can fall behind. Dead rows accumulate as table bloat. The file grows, but since VACUUM can only mark that space as internally reusable, it doesn't shrink the table or return space to the OS. To actually reclaim disk space, you need to rebuild the table.
How do you know if you have a bloat problem? You can do a quick check using pg_stat_user_tables. The tuple counts are estimates, but this is one good diagnostic signal.
SELECT
schemaname,
relname,
pg_size_pretty(pg_relation_size(schemaname || '.' || relname)) AS size,
n_live_tup,
n_dead_tup,
CASE WHEN n_live_tup > 0
THEN round((n_dead_tup::float / n_live_tup::float)::numeric, 4)
END AS dead_tup_ratio,
last_autovacuum,
last_autoanalyze
FROM pg_stat_user_tables
ORDER BY dead_tup_ratio DESC NULLS LAST;
(Query adapted from Crunchy Data's bloat checking guide )
A rough rule of thumb:
Below 50% bloat : Generally acceptable. Monitor it and check autovacuum settings, but no urgent action needed.
Above 50% bloat : You're likely wasting disk space and paying a performance cost from extra page reads. It's at least worth investigating — and possibly addressing — if you see slow queries or growing table sizes.
There is no single bloat percentage that determines whether a table needs attention. Consider wasted bytes, workload, growth, and whether reclaiming space is worth the rewrite.
How pg_repack works
The pg_repack extension was the option for online table rebuilds for years. Here's how it works:
External tool : pg_repack runs as a command-line utility (pg_repack --table my_table -d mydb) from an external server or management host. You needed to install both the extension inside Postgres (CREATE EXTENSION pg_repack) and the client binary on whatever machine would run it.
Trigger-based change capture : It creates a log table and installs triggers on your target table to capture all INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE operations during the rebuild. This adds trigger overhead on every write for the duration of the operation.
Shadow table approach : It creates a new copy of the table, populates it from the original, replays the trigger log, then does a brief lock-and-swap, along with a final table rename.
This worked well, and many production systems relied on it for years. But installing third-party extensions makes some teams nervous, and the external binary adds operational overhead.
How pg_squeeze works
pg_squeeze (from CYBERTEC, the same team behind much of the Postgres 19 REPACK work) came along and took a more modern approach. It's also seen wide production use.
Logical decoding : pg_squeeze uses Postgres’ WAL-based logical decoding to capture concurrent changes. This means no triggers are installed on your table. This is the same approach that PG 19's built-in REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) now uses.
Background worker : This runs entirely inside the database as a background worker process which means unlike pg_repack, you don’t need an external CLI tool. You can also configure it to run automatically when bloat thresholds are exceeded.
Still an extension : Lots of folks prefer a built-in option, but this still requires wal_level = logical, a replication slot, compiling and installing the extension, and adding it to shared_preload_libraries.
pg_squeeze in a sense is the prototype for what became PG 19's REPACK (CONCURRENTLY). The built-in version inherits the logical decoding approach but integrates it directly into the server without an extension, shared_preload_libraries, or separate configuration tables.
Enter REPACK
Postgres 19 adds REPACK as a first-class SQL command with three modes:
-- Basic repack, like VACUUM FULL — takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock
REPACK my_table;
-- Online repack using CONCURRENTLY just like you would with indexes
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) my_table;
-- Online repack + reorder by index
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) my_table USING INDEX my_index;
REPACK (CONCURRENTLY)
This is what makes the feature production-ready. With CONCURRENTLY, the ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock

Have you ever wondered how objects from our daily lives are designed? How can we generate a computer 3D model of a mug, a bottle of Diet Coke, or a Saturn V rocket? What about designing the blades of a jet engine? A test dummy? How about making an animation of a LEGO house building itself? Or making a realistic render of a bowl of fruit? In this workshop, you will learn skills to design all these and much more!
How to CAD Almost Anything introduces students to CAD (Computer-Aided Design) through various fun examples focused on reverse engineering. In contrast to traditional mechanical design courses, this workshop emphasizes the design process itself, understanding how to plan and best leverage our available tools to arrive at our desired result. Thus, the sessions are less about following the instructions on an engineering drawing and more about independent thinking and strategizing, such as reverse engineering an object into a 3D model.
Come and learn how to CAD almost anything!
This supplemental resource offers links to the class’s Solidworks , Creo , Fusion , Inventor, Onshape , and NX website materials, as well as companion playlists of the Solidworks , Creo , Fusion, Inventor , Onshape , and NX session recordings on YouTube.

hn.title: The Strongest Sokoban Solver
hn.text:
Soksolv solves more levels than any published Sokoban solver on both standard benchmark suites, including 24 world-first automated level solves. It's also faster on the levels that other solvers solve (~3.2x in total time).
Large Test Suite · % of 3,272 levels solved
Open Test Suite · % of 10,043 levels solved
soksolv Festival Sokolution Takaken YASS BoxSearch
Festival: measured on the same hardware. Others: published results. Log scale of what's left unsolved.
As is common for this era, I did not handwrite a single line of code. I used one long Opus 5.5 session in Claude Code, along with ~430 subagents (a mixture of Sonnet 5.5, Opus 5.5, and Fable 5.2) for an API-equivalent cost ~$3,500 (I used the $100 plan, and a reset).
I ran the 14-day long Claude session from my MacBook and did ~50% of the work on-the-go by dictating to my iPhone via /remote-control . On the compute side, I needed 15,000 vCPU-hours (AMD EPYC) to do research and verification runs, as well as the (very) long benchmark runs.
Sokoban Quick Tour
First published in Japan in 1982, Sokoban is a puzzle game where you push boxes onto goals. It was proven PSPACE-complete in 1997, and small boards hide massive search spaces. Human-solvable levels commonly need hundreds to thousands of moves.
Below is the solution for Microban #1 .
worker: pushes one box at a time box: can be pushed, not pulled goal: every box must end on one box on a goal
0

0
pushes
solved
Levels are Adversarial
Sokoban levels can be explored as a cyclic graph of moves. With a branching factor of ~16 (but up to ~176 on huge boards!), any kind of brute forcing becomes unviable after a handful of moves.
As a player, and especially as a solver author, Sokoban levels feel adversarial by design. Any obvious heuristic is immediately punished by the game rules or the level author.
When I wrote my first Sokoban solver (~4 years ago), I tried to encode how I thought I was playing the game. Without thinking too hard, we can describe this as "get the boxes to the goals". Okay, so, how do we calculate that in a program? Maybe the sum of box-to-goal distances?
Using this as a guide, we can explore the graph of possible moves and see what happens.
greedy: most boxes on goals first
push 0
boxes on goals after each push
0 1
solution
push 0
boxes on goals after each push
0 0 0 1 1 2
Ah, by prioritizing boxes on goals we walk right into a trap. The game becomes deadlocked and unsolvable, and our solver with a single rule runs until the end-of-time with no solution.
We'll need to come up with a bag of strategies to perform better than even novice players.
Laying Out the Project
I've been using frontier agents at work for a while now and I enjoy (and get a lot of profit from) what I call "creative goal setting". Where you define the goal, parts of the path, risks that you consider acceptable, and some preferences on the method.
What I've experienced, is that agents are really great hill-climbers, and a solver program is the purest hill there is. There are two things to measure: the number of levels solved, and some kind of aggregate time of those solutions.
At the beginning of this project, I started a Claude Code session and defined a hill climbing plan. One immutable incumbent version of the solver (the first version was just a brute force search), one hypothesis per experiment, a frozen verifier (so agents don't cheat), and separate promotion suites.
As I continued to make progress, I expanded the pool of levels that I measured my solver against until I was taking on the two common benchmarks used in the Sokoban solver community; the Large Test Suite and the Open Test Suite, which contain increasingly complex Sokoban levels. There are some duplicate levels between the suites with a unique count of 9,756 total levels, with an average of 16 boxes, and ~830 moves (~160 pushes) to solve each.
I knew that I didn't want to build on top of an existing solver for two reasons. The first was that I did this project because I love this kinda stuff, and it's a less interesting journey to make small patches to an existing program. It's much more fun to be part of something from scratch and to live the narrative of it.
The second reason, that I didn't realize until the ending stages of the project, was that if you build on top of existing solution, you become extremely tied to certain design decisions without the knowledge of those decisions, and it becomes impossible to make improvements beyond one order of magnitude.
So I set some initial ground rules for the agents. No machine learning (much harder for me to audit), no reading the code of rival solvers (or we risk copying inefficient designs), and no hardcoding to solve levels (that's cheating).
At the beginning of the project, I was concerned about agents cheating. I'm sure we all remember early LLM generations that would just comment out tests to achieve their given goals!
But I found no signs of agents cheating at all. My best guess for this is that I steered agent motivation towards experimentation and learning rather than it being a pure numbers game.
Two more ground rules that I set were: the solver must be written in Go (I find it fun to read), and a 15 GB memory cap so it fits on an 8-core/16 GB machine. I also wanted to use the same cores as Festival (the leading rival solver) for matters of fairness.
During the iteration cycle, each solution was replayed move by move on the original level using the frozen verifier.

E.1. Release 19 #
E.1.1. Overview
E.1.2. Migration to Version 19
E.1.3. Changes
E.1.4. Acknowledgments
Release date: 2026-11-19
E.1.1. Overview #
PostgreSQL 19 contains many new features and enhancements, including:
New REPACK command that reclaims disk space and reorganizes table contents, which can improve query performance. REPACK (CONCURRENTLY) allows repacking without blocking reads and writes to the table.
pg_plan_advice extension for controlling query planner decisions and pg_stash_advice extension that applies plan advice automatically based on the query.
Better performance in many areas, including automatic scaling of the number of I/O worker processes, quicker foreign-key checks, and further planning and execution optimizations.
Logical replication can now be enabled without a server restart when wal_level is set to replica .
Logical replication of sequence values .
Support for “ read-your-writes ” consistency on standbys via the new WAIT command.
Parallel autovacuum of table indexes and autovacuum prioritization through a new scoring system.
The above items and other new features of PostgreSQL 19 are explained in more detail in the sections below.
E.1.2. Migration to Version 19 #
A dump/restore using pg_dumpall or use of pg_upgrade or logical replication is required for those wishing to migrate data from any previous release. See Section 18.6 for general information on migrating to new major releases.
Version 19 contains a number of changes that may affect compatibility with previous releases. Observe the following incompatibilities:
Add server variable password_expiration_warning_threshold to warn about password expiration (Gilles Darold, Nathan Bossart) §
The default warning period is seven days.
Issue a warning after successful MD5 password authentication (Nathan Bossart) §
The warning can be disabled via server variable md5_password_warnings . MD5 passwords were marked as deprecated in PostgreSQL 18.
Remove RADIUS support (Thomas Munro) §
PostgreSQL only supported RADIUS over UDP , which is unfixably insecure.
Force standard_conforming_strings to always be on in the database server (Tom Lane) §
Dumps created using pre- PostgreSQL 19 versions of pg_dump or pg_dumpall , and using standard_conforming_strings = off , will not properly load into PostgreSQL 19 and later servers. Users should create dumps using PostgreSQL 19 or later versions of these applications, or use standard_conforming_strings = on .
Client applications still support operations with servers having standard_conforming_strings = off , for compatibility with old servers. The server variable escape_string_warning has been removed as unnecessary.
Disallow carriage returns and line feeds in database, role, and tablespace names (Mahendra Singh Thalor) §
pg_upgrade will also disallow upgrading of clusters that use such names. This was changed to avoid security problems.
Change the default index opclasses for inet and cidr data types from btree_gist to GiST (Tom Lane) § §
The btree_gist inet / cidr opclasses are broken because they can exclude rows that should be returned. pg_upgrade will disallow upgrading of clusters with btree_gist inet / cidr indexes.
Disallow system columns from being used in COPY FROM ... WHERE (Tom Lane) §
The values of such columns were not well-defined.
Change a json_array() call which returns no rows to return an empty JSON array (Richard Guo) §
This previously returned NULL .
Cause transactions to pass their READ ONLY and DEFERRABLE status to postgres_fdw sessions (Etsuro Fujita) §
This means READ ONLY transactions can no longer modify rows processed by postgres_fdw sessions.
Change default of max_locks_per_transaction from 64 to 128 (Heikki Linnakangas) §
Lock size allocation has changed, so effectively settings must now be doubled to match their capacity in previous releases.
Remove server variable io_workers (Thomas Munro) §
This has been replaced by four new variables; see Section E.1.3.1.2 .
Change JIT to be disabled by default (Jelte Fennema-Nio) §
Previously JIT was enabled by default, and activated based on optimizer costs, but this costing has been determined to be unreliable. This change requires sites that are doing many large analytical queries to manually enable JIT .
Change parallel vacuum leaders and workers to share the cost-based vacuum delay limit (Bharath Rupireddy) §
Previously each worker process slept based only on the cost it incurred itself, so a parallel vacuum could consume several times the budget set by vacuum_cost_limit . With this change, VACUUM with parallel workers and cost-based delay enabled might run slower than in previous releases.
Rename column sync_error_count to sync_table_error_count in system view pg_stat_subscription_stats (Vignesh C) §
This is necessary since sequence errors are now tracked separately.
Rename wait event type BUFFERPIN to BUFFER and rename wait event BufferPin to BufferCleanup (Andres Freund) §
Remove wait event BufferContent and add more precise wait events BufferShared , BufferShareExclusive , and BufferExclusive (Andres Freund) §
Change index access method handlers to use a static IndexAmRoutines structure, rather than dynamically allocated ones (Matthias van de Meent) §
Remove optimizer hook get_relation_info_hook and add better-placed hook build_simple_rel_hook (Robert Haas) §
Change psql 's \crosstabview command to honor the \pset null setting (Chao Li) §
Change full text search and pg_trgm to use the database's locale provider for character classification when parsing text (Jeff Davis) §
Previously, characters were classified using libc, regardless of the locale provider. In databases with a locale provider other than libc (e.g., ICU , builtin ) and where the locale configured through that local

hn.title: What Comes After AGI?
hn.text:
Your browser does not support the video tag.
For decades, AI research has been focused on a monumental milestone: building artificial general intelligence, or AGI - machines that match humans across nearly all cognitive tasks. It was always clear that, in principle, intelligence could progress beyond human level, but the prospect of AGI was far enough off, and surrounded by ample uncertainties of its own, that looking past it felt premature.
Now that AGI is coming within reach, we can no longer put off seriously considering what comes next. While far from certain, AI could continue to advance at its current pace - and possibly even accelerate - towards artificial general superintelligence, or ASI. It could have a profound impact on science, the economy, and society at a scale and speed much greater than AGI itself. Preparing for that potential shift requires mapping the possible roads from AGI to ASI and building rigorous, reliable ways to track progress.
The continuum of general intelligence
To examine how the development of advanced AI might unfold, it helps to think of general intelligence , whether biological or artificial, as existing on a continuum. Human-level AGI is just one point along that spectrum.
ASI sits further along as an advanced system that consistently outperforms large groups of human experts on tasks that could take them years to complete, using fewer resources and less time. Examples would be making the same scientific progress as an entire research field in a fraction of the time, or achieving technological developments, such as in chip design, on par with what large companies can do in a year. ASI would need to meet this bar across virtually all tasks of human interest, not just some in narrow domains (which is already the case with some AI systems today that can beat any human in Chess and Go, predict the structure of proteins from their amino acid sequences, or prove theorems that resisted human mathematicians for decades).
Interestingly, we have a good mathematical understanding of the very upper end of the intelligence continuum - the theoretical limits of general intelligence. We also know about hard physical, logical, and complexity-theoretic limits to what AI can achieve, such as predicting how real-world complex systems - from climate to immune systems to human societies - play out with arbitrary precision.
Yet knowing those upper limits doesn’t tell us what comes before them. Even in theory, it’s hard to predict how capable a ‘good enough’ approximation of general intelligence can be. For example, solving chess perfectly requires far more computing power than exists on Earth, yet a thumbnail-sized chip can play the game well enough to defeat any human.
What we do know is that fundamental limits lie far beyond both today’s AI systems and humans. But the vast space between human-level AI and theoretical limits to intelligence, which encompasses expert AGI and a whole regime of more and more advanced superintelligent systems, is largely uncharted.
Cognitive industrialization
Even if you are pessimistic that progress at the frontier of AI capabilities will continue, consider what happens if AI hardware and software continue to become more efficient.
Over the last ten years, AI progress was fueled by steady growth in effective compute , driven by three compounding factors:
Hardware manufacturing improvements: Under Moore's law and related trends, compute per dollar has increased by roughly 1.5x per year for six decades - meaning the same investment 18 months from now buys twice the compute.
Algorithmic efficiency: The amount of training compute (FLOPs) required to reach a fixed AI performance level has fallen at roughly 3–6x per year over the last decade , while algorithmic efficiency at inference improved by roughly 3x per year. Doubling efficiency is practically equivalent to doubling the stock of physical compute.
Compute hardware investment: Spending on AI hardware has grown by roughly 2.5x per year over the past decade. For example, the training compute of the largest frontier training runs grows by more than 4x per year .
Multiplying all three factors gives an overall growth rate of global effective compute stock of at least 10x per year - a factor of 10 billion over ten years. Imagine that this trend holds. A decade from now, for each single AI agent you could run today, you would hypothetically be able to run more agents of the same quality than there are people in the world.
At the same time, continued hardware and software (inference) efficiency improvements alone would reduce the compute demand to run an AI workload by about 4x per year . A cognitive workload that can be performed by today’s AI systems for $1 billion in compute tokens would cost just $1000 in ten years. Looking only at the last few years gives even steeper estimates: a recent Epoch study finds the consumer price for achieving a fixed score on a set of benchmarks has fallen by more than 13x per year since 2023.
Extrapolating both trends into the next decade raises the prospect of a dramatically larger global effective compute stock combined with equally dramatic cost reductions for cognitive work performed by AI. Increasingly, many cognitive tasks may therefore soon become commoditised . Much like mechanical industrialization turned routine physical labor into a commodity, this shift will lead to cognitive industrialization characterized by rapidly increasing standardization and automation of cognitive work across sectors, industrial-scale infrastructure build-out, and an abundance of (certain) cognitive outputs and services.
Is such a dramatic proliferation of intelligence realistic? It’s certainly not a given , but practical ceilings on compute build-out , and more speculative ceilings on algorithmic efficiency, together might allow the effective population of today’s AI agents to scale up by more than a thousand-fold by 2030, and more than a billion-fold within ten years from now.

hn.title: "I can tell you wrote this yourself"
hn.text:
"I can tell you wrote this yourself"
19 Nov, 2026
Those were some of the first words my honours project supervisor said to me last week when we met to discuss a progress report I had written to mark the midway point of the project.
It's a roughly 10-page report on the control of flapping-wing micro aerial vehicles - which is probably very boring unless you're particularly interested in that. I accidentally set the due date for the report a week early in my calendar, so after spending 48 hours stressed and pumping out 5,000 words, citing references and adding diagrams 1 , I was pleasantly relieved to find I'd tricked myself into being quite productive. I had a lot of time to get my supervisor to review the report and action his feedback.
When he told me he could tell I wrote it myself, I wasn't sure how to take it. A compliment? An insult? Then he followed it up with:
"I've been sent a lot of reports written by AI."
At first this shocked me. Our reports are limited to 10 pages - so the appendices are getting a big workout around here - how hard is it to right 10 pages yourself?
But then I thought about what the last year of my engineering degree has been like.
Assignment documents that start with "you are strongly encouraged to explore the use of AI" which quickly turns into the clear understanding that you aren't just encouraged but expected to use it. That you're disadvantaged by not using it. The hardest class of my degree was spent in a brick-walled windowless computer lab prompting an AI for eight hours a day.
The reason why we've been pushed to use it?
Apparently it's the way the industry is going. Apparently actually knowing things doesn't matter nearly so much as knowing how to prompt a machine to do the thing. Apparently the future of engineering - at least in my field - is to become a glorified babysitter. The AI isn't going anywhere, they say, so it's best we learn how to manage it well.
But sitting in a room telling an AI "ignore the approaching deadline, we still have 8 hours, keep working" isn't exactly filling me with enthusiasm for the rest of my career.
It's soul crushing, and I don't want to outsource so much of my thinking to it.
In a world where people are using AI to summarise books instead of reading them and turning to AI for therapy , I don't want to keep using it. It feels like such a slippery slope. As literacy and numeracy rates decline , I can't help but question whether encouraging us to rely on AI so heavily is a good idea.
It makes me wonder: are we still thinking for ourselves at all?
Because I worry that it starts with using it for an assignment when you're encouraged to, but then it turns into relying on it to write a 10-page report on a project you should know back-to-front. A project that you'll have to present and defend in person when it finishes. And then you're asking it for advice, using it to summarise books, turning to it for anything you would normally look up or ask a friend.
The internet is riddled with AI content that is making it increasingly more difficult to tell fact from fiction. In a world where everything is so polarised and deliberately provoking, the ability to identify bias or motivation in the content we consume has perhaps never been more important. Being able to think for ourselves has perhaps never been more important.
As the tech world continues to offer us increasingly more opportunities to automate things, I'm practically begging you to please not automate your thinking.
Read the books. Write the papers. Search for answers instead of asking AI. Ask a friend. Ask your mum about the mystery illness you're convinced you're developing and then take her advice and try drinking a glass of water.
Think about what the creators of the content you consume want you to think 2 . Treat the things you consume like the Year 7 English class where you were taught how to identify persuasive techniques. Think about things as much as possible.
Please just don't get the AI do it for you.
On a more positive note, here's some recent good things:
Got to see a tawny frogmouth up close recently - in the middle of the day! One has nested in a tree near the university's engineering precinct.
Finished my final assessment for the semester today! Officially only one semester to go! Went and saw 'You Can See Everything' with Han last week and I can't stop talking and thinking about it. If you've seen it, please talk to me about it. If you haven't seen it, please go and see it!
Felt homesick the other day and made Mum's scalloped potatoes recipe! SO good.
The weather has been beautiful lately. Morning runs and walks have been extra fun. The other morning I ran past a guy walking barefoot through the park with a CAT in his backpack.
Made plans with Bec & Han to see 'Sunrise On The Reaping' next Monday - no spoilers if you've already seen it! Keen to talk about it after then.
Anyhow, happy almost-weekend!
-- Em
Subscribe to my blog

I think what I want you to think here is probably pretty obvious. ↩

hn.title: Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
hn.text:
Vint Cerf on why TCP/IP was never patented
Future Stories, my new podcast about technology, science and the way we live, starts today. The first guest is one of the people who built the Internet.
João Tomé
Nov 19, 2026
2
4
Share
EXTRA, extra! Today I’m launching Future Stories, my own podcast about technology, science and the way we live.
The first guest is Vint Cerf . He co-designed TCP/IP with Bob Kahn in the 1970s, the rules that let the world’s networks talk to each other. Interviewing him was on my bucket list for years. When I was at Cloudflare I thought about asking him many times, but I was a bit shy. He’s Vint Cerf, after all. This year I finally asked, and he said yes.
We talked over Zoom (not using Zoom again) on October 14. He’s 83, he left Google this year after more than twenty years, and he’s helping start a company, Tolero, that is building software for an Internet between planets. His words: “the speed of light is too slow.”
“Who will our allies be 25 years from now? And we didn’t know. So we thought the only way we can be assured that the allies will have access to this is to simply open it up.”
Some peculiar stories from the conversation
First, a bug related one (ring a bell? those never stopped over the years…) . Vint once spent two weeks on a program that failed at random, so he couldn’t reproduce it. He finally asked his best friend, Steve Crocker, to step through it with him. At one point Crocker said “that’s the problem”, and he was right. Thirty seconds, after two weeks. Vint’s takeaway is that this is why collaboration matters.
Then a bottle of glitter . In late 1989 three commercial Internet services started in the United States, and one of them was called CERFnet , in San Diego. They first wanted to call it SURFnet , because surfing the Internet, but a network in the Netherlands had a name too close to it. So they asked Vint if they could use his.
He had a moment of “what if they screw it up?” , then decided that people name kids after other people and nobody blames the person they were named after. At the launch, he and the network’s director smashed a plastic bottle of glitter over a Cisco router.
He also tried to connect Minitel , the French online service, to MCI Mail, the email service he built in the 1980s. MCI Mail was designed to link to everything. It reached the telegraph system, which he calls 19th-century stuff, and fax. It even reached the post office: type a postal address into the email and they printed it, put it in an envelope and mailed it. Minitel refused to connect, and he says he still doesn’t understand why.
One more, from outside the interview: In 2020, someone on the Internet-history mailing list (I’m on it) asked if anyone had ever seen Vint without a three-piece suit. One reply: “I have seen Vint in a t-shirt!” Vint answered with just a photo, “IP on Everything”, from a 1992 engineers’ meeting where, in his words, he “felt compelled” to do an “IP on Everything” striptease. The thread is public .
We didn’t go very deep into AI. Time was short, and it’s not his main field these days. But even there, he has a clear way of thinking about it. And near the end he shows a piece of the original ARPANET on camera, and talks about his worry that the next century won’t be able to read what we leave behind.
Vint Cerf shows a plaque from the ARPANET’s Interface Message Processor, the refrigerator-sized computer that was the network’s packet switch. It was given to him when he left ARPA in 1982. The hardware dates from 1969.
“I’m worried that the 22nd century won’t know what happened in the 21st because all of our records will have evaporated or will be uninterpretable.”
The full conversation is 56 minutes, with chapters:
You can also read the transcript at ourfuturestories.eu/vint-cerf , or listen in your favourite podcast app: ourfuturestories.eu/subscribe . A Portuguese article about it is on SAPO . Short clips are coming in the next days.
This is a passion project. The idea is to tell good stories, the kind that hold up over time. If you like it, subscribe, share it with a friend, and tell me who I should talk to next, you can do it here: ourfuturestories.eu/#contact .
Stay tuned, geek out!
ourfuturestories.eu/subscribe
———
Fun fact: in 2024 I did a segment on the 50 years of the TCP paper on my previous podcast, This Week in NET at Cloudflare. My guests were three then-colleagues: Mark Nottingham (standards), Marwan Fayed (research) and Lucas Pardue (web protocols, co-chair of the IETF’s QUIC working group). You can listen here (or below).
The paper is “A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication”, by Vint Cerf and Bob Kahn, published in May 1974 in IEEE Transactions on Communications. It described TCP, a way to join many packet networks into a network of networks. TCP was later split into TCP and IP, and in 1983 they became the core of the Internet that DARPA launched.

hn.title: The 98% Slot Machine: How Paid Advertising Became an Extraction Tax
Anthropic’s Nasdaq debut
Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
Bit Shifting in Basic
hn.text:
VIC-20 character blocks, bit shifted.
Recently, I had the urge to be lazy and have the computer do my work for me. I was designing some 8×8 graphics characters for the Commodore VIC-20 and wanted one for each offset position in a 2-character block (see image to the right).
Using modern tools like the Windows-based CBM prg Studio I could have easily edited each one by hand to get the desired result (which is what I did to create that image), but I thought it might be more fun to just design one character and write a program to create the other shifted frames.
I have bit shifted in C programming many times (because it has a bit shift operator) but I don’t recall ever knowingly doing it in BASIC.
Bit shifting basics
Bit shifting is where you take all the bits in a byte (or word, or long, whatever) and move them left or right. Here is an example of shifting the byte value 00111100 to the right:
Before: [ 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 0 ]
After : [ 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0 ] If you just want to shift and don’t care about the bit that “falls off the edge,” it is as simple as multiplying or dividing the value by 2.
To demonstrate this, we first need a program that will display a byte as bits.
0 REM bitsslow.bas
10 Z=&H00:GOSUB 500
20 Z=&HF0:GOSUB 500
30 Z=&H0F:GOSUB 500
40 Z=&HFF:GOSUB 500
50 END
500 REM PRINT BITS
510 FOR ZB=7 TO 0 STEP -1
520 IF Z AND 2^ZB THEN PRINT"1"; ELSE PRINT "0";
530 NEXT
540 PRINT:RETURN
The routine at line 500 will print the value in variable Z as bits. It is hard coded to only work with a byte (0-255). When I run that, this is what it displays:
00000000
11110000
00001111
11111111 Those lines correspond to &H00, &HF0, &H0F and &FF. I show them in hex so the bit pattern is easier to see (0=0000, F=1111).
A bit faster…
My bit printing routine is so slow that you can see it print the digits one at a time. This is due to the math that goes on in line 520 for each bit check. To speed things up, we could pre-calculate an array of those powers of two (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128) and use that instead:
0 REM bitsfast.bas
5 GOSUB 1000
10 Z=&H00:GOSUB 500
20 Z=&HF0:GOSUB 500
30 Z=&H0F:GOSUB 500
40 Z=&HFF:GOSUB 500
50 END
500 REM PRINT BITS
510 FOR ZB=7 TO 0 STEP -1
520 IF Z AND ZB(ZB) THEN PRINT"1"; ELSE PRINT "0";
530 NEXT
540 PRINT:RETURN
1000 REM INIT BIT ARRAY
1010 FOR ZB=0 TO 7
1020 ZB(ZB)=2^ZB
1030 NEXT
1040 RETURN
Line 5 will GOSUB to our initialization routine which sets up the power-of-two array ZB(). After that, the routine at 500 can be called as it previously was, except now it will print so fast you can’t really see it printing.
Now let’s use this routine to demonstrate bit shifting by multiplying or dividing by 2.
Bit shifting left
0 REM bitshftl.bas
5 GOSUB 1000
10 Z=1 '00000001
20 FOR A=1 TO 8
30 GOSUB 500
35 REM *2 TO SHIFT LEFT
40 Z=Z*2:NEXT
50 END
500 REM PRINT BITS
510 FOR ZB=7 TO 0 STEP -1
520 IF Z AND ZB(ZB) THEN PRINT"1"; ELSE PRINT "0";
530 NEXT
540 PRINT:RETURN
1000 REM INIT BIT ARRAY
1010 FOR ZB=0 TO 7
1020 ZB(ZB)=2^ZB
1030 NEXT
1040 RETURN In line 10, Z starts out with 1, which is the bit pattern of 00000001. It is then multiplied by 2 in a loop eight times, each time shifting the bit one place to the left. The output looks like this:
00000001
00000010
00000100
00001000
00010000
00100000
01000000
10000000 Bit shifting right
And if we start out with Z being 128 (bit pattern 10000000) and divide by 2, it will shift right:
0 REM bitshftr.bas
5 GOSUB 1000
10 Z=128 '10000000
20 FOR A=1 TO 8
30 GOSUB 500
35 REM /2 TO SHIFT RIGHT
40 Z=Z/2:NEXT
50 END
500 REM PRINT BITS
510 FOR ZB=7 TO 0 STEP -1
520 IF Z AND ZB(ZB) THEN PRINT"1"; ELSE PRINT "0";
530 NEXT
540 PRINT:RETURN
1000 REM INIT BIT ARRAY
1010 FOR ZB=0 TO 7
1020 ZB(ZB)=2^ZB
1030 NEXT
1040 RETURN
This will display:
10000000
01000000
00100000
00010000
00001000
00000100
00000010
00000001 Pretty simple. And if that were all I wanted to do, I’d be done.
But that was not all I wanted to do, so I am not done.
I wanted to shift bits right in one byte and have the bits that shift out end up shifting in to a second byte, like this:
1st Byte 2nd Byte
1) [00001111][00000000]
2) [00000111][10000000]
3) [00000011][11000000]
4) [00000011][11100000]
5) [00000001][11110000]
6) [00000000][11111000]
...etc... I spent far too much time coming up with an approach that would get me which bits were going to be shifted off to the right (using AND), and then placing those in a new variable and then shifting those bits to the left to line up where they would have ended up if I had just shifted a 16-bit value…
…then I realized that was silly, because I could just use a 16-bit value in BASIC!
16-bits in BASIC
You may have seen things like this which print out memory locations BASIC is using:
PRINT PEEK(25)*256+PEEK(26) In Color BASIC, memory locations 25 and 26 contain the 16-bit address for where BASIC memory starts. Since PEEK only works on a single byte, it takes two PEEKs to get the two bytes that make up the 16-byte address, and some math to turn the two 8-bit values into one 16-bit value.
On my virtual CoCo in the Xroar emulator, memory location 25 contains 38 (&H26) and memory location 26 contains 1 (&h01). To turn those two 8-bit values into a 16-bit address, I need to somehow shift the 38/&H28 left eight times into a new 16-bit value, and then add (or OR) in the 1/&H01 value.
In C, one of the ways we’d do this is by using the bit shift operator:
uint16_t Result;
uint8_2 Byte1;
uint8_2 Byte2;
Byte1 = Peek(25); // Made up function to get a memory value.
Byte2 = Peek(26);
Result = (Byte1 << 8) | Byte2; // Shift Byte1 left 8 bits,
// OR in Byte2.
// Or...
Result = (Byte1 << 8) + Byte2; // Since the right 8 bits are empty,
// adding would have the same result.
…but there are many other ways to do the same thing, some much faster than these two approaches.
Back to BASIC
Shifting left can be done by multiplying the value by 2. To shift once, you might have:
V = V * 2 To shift twice, you could do:
V = V * 2 * 2 …but that looks silly. You’d just multiply

hn.title: Weight-Space Programming builds neural networks like a 1990s researcher
hn.text:
Weight-Space Programming builds neural networks like a 1990s researcher
The writing aspect of WSP turns out to be quite a history lesson.
Lex Toumbourou · Nov 18, 2026
LLMs Interpretability
Intro
Weight-Space Programming still has me pretty intrigued. The basic idea is that frontier LLMs can read, write and edit the weights of neural networks. There's nuance to what's going on, but it feels like there's a lot of new ground to explore.
In the original blog post , beyond the reading and editing experiments, the authors had GPT-6 Astra build a network to play Go from scratch, then improve it by playing practice games, and editing the weights based on analysis of its losses. That loop of writing, testing and editing feels like a new way to train a network, something like LLM Descent . But is it?
In this article, I run my own weight-writing experiment with Claude Fable 5.2 on a familiar image classification problem. Look closely at what the model builds, and it turns out to be an interesting lesson in historical model-building techniques. With that new lens on weight-space programming, I also study the Go network that Astra built in the original article, and find something very similar.
Building an image classifier with LLM Descent
MNIST is the OG image classification problem. The goal is to label each handwritten digit, 0 to 9.
Similar to the Go test in the original Weight-Space Programming post, I built a test with a fixed CNN , then prompted Claude to write code that sets all its weights from scratch, with a few rules that include no fitting, regression, or searching. Drawing filters and templates by hand, from formulas or strokes, is explicitly allowed.
It's a considerably stricter setup than Astra had for Go, with no PyTorch and no practice games, only its training loss, accuracy and confusion matrix after each attempt. The tests in this blog post were run with Claude Fable 5.2, which performed much better than Opus 5.5.
Claude starts with no weights at all, and has to set every one of this network's 5,994 weights "by hand":
model = nn . Sequential (
nn . Conv2d ( 1 , 8 , 5 ), # conv1: 1x28x28 -> 8x24x24
nn . ReLU (),
nn . MaxPool2d ( 2 ), # 8x24x24 -> 8x12x12
nn . Conv2d ( 8 , 16 , 5 ), # conv2: 8x12x12 -> 16x8x8
nn . ReLU (),
nn . MaxPool2d ( 2 ), # 16x8x8 -> 16x4x4
nn . Flatten (), # 16x4x4 -> 256
nn . Linear ( 256 , 10 ), # fc: 256 -> 10 class logits
)
You can read the whole prompt on GitHub.
Claude's code runs in a sandbox that can only import NumPy, SciPy and math. Once it returns the weights, a test harness runs the network on the training and test images.
Claude has up to 50 steps, and at each one it sees all the feedback so far. The training set is 10,000 images from MNIST's official training split. Claude never sees the 10,000 official test images or how it scores on them, and the network with the lowest training loss gives us the final test score.
Here's an example of the feedback it gets after its first attempt:
Step 1 of 50: training loss 1.0324, accuracy 0.7147.
Confusion matrix (rows: true digit, columns: predicted digit):

1 4 1022 23 0 3 4 0 8 0 0
2 30 5 461 176 3 12 9 13 271 10
3 2 0 8 687 0 125 51 4 133 20
4 7 19 14 6 768 0 35 10 22 102
5 10 5 13 45 2 492 312 6 29 1
6 41 17 19 1 266 8 603 0 10 2
7 8 2 21 45 2 7 13 906 11 75
8 15 19 86 5 5 4 60 27 714 74
9 15 9 1 4 1 19 46 82 13 771
History (training set, 10,000 images):
step | loss | accuracy
---- | ---- | --------
1 | 1.0324 | 0.7147
At most 49 steps left. Reply with the complete build_weights() for step 2
in one Python code block.
The descent
I ran it three times.
Though I have early stopping configured to stop when the training loss stops improving, all three runs descend for the full 50 steps, still improving when they run out, and land around 90% on the test set. Amazingly, that's close to where a training run with Adam gets to after 50 gradient steps.
A 1990s computer-vision pipeline
In 1998, LeCun's paper that introduced MNIST described that era's approaches thus far as "a fixed feature extractor and a trainable classifier", where the feature extractor "is often entirely hand crafted" (LeCun et al., 1998) . Accuracy, he wrote, "is largely determined by the ability of the designer to come up with an appropriate set of features", which is "a daunting task which, unfortunately, must be redone for each new problem."
That daunting task is exactly what Claude takes on. All three runs built the same kind of pipeline, though not from the same parts:

Let's follow run 1, step by step, based on Claude's replies and reasoning. It's the best of the three, at 91.3%, but the other two follow a similar path, measuring their way from hand-drawn templates to a classifier.
1. Hand-drawn templates (steps 1 to 3)
Claude starts like a 1990s computer vision engineer. Its first layer is a set of line detectors at four angles, written from formulas. They're cousins of the Sobel filter , a classic way to find edges in an image, which 1990s digit recognisers started with (Favata and Srikantan, 1996) .
Each detector is a 5×5 grid of weights in the first convolutional layer . The way a conv layer works is that each filter slides across the image, multiplying the 25 pixels under it by its 25 weights and adding them up, so it scores high wherever there's a stroke at its angle, and zero on blank paper. Fable fills in four of the layer's eight filters this way and leaves the other four at zero for later.

hn.title: Show HN: Foolscap – a writing app that reads your book and never writes for you
hn.text:
People are scared of their ability to write and think atrophying, so I wondered: what if I built something that enhanced human creativity instead of destroying it by doing the thinking and writing for people? Foolscap is the result, or at least the first version of that idea that's fleshed out enough to share here. It reads as you write and picks out the structure: characters, ideas, threads, what's left hanging. You can respond to what it picks out, so there's a dialectic between the system and you as the writer. There's also an agent on the side, plugged into the same system, so you can ask about your book and fire off actions through conversation. It never writes into your work. The system can also follow theorems and proofs and string together their dependencies, but I haven't made that a focus yet. There's no Lean support, for example. If anyone's interested in that, I'd love to hear it. I want to build this by iterating with the people who use it: a tool that uses AI not to bypass the creative process, but to bring new tools to it. There's a free tier, and if you email hello@foolscap.works I'll send you a code for 50% off. This is my first product, so feedback of any kind is welcome. Thanks,
David

On 13 November 2026 the President of the Court decided to exclude a Romanian lawyer from representing or otherwise assisting litigants before the Court, for a period of two years.
This came after the Chamber that was dealing with the application in which the lawyer was acting as one of two representatives found that the observations which she had submitted on the case contained numerous errors concerning the Court’s case-law. These included the citation of non-existent (“hallucinated”) cases; the citation of fictitious paragraphs in genuine judgments and decisions of the Court; and the citation of existing case-law that was irrelevant to the propositions advanced or that plainly contradicted the submissions they were intended to support.
The lawyer acknowledged that she had used Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools to draft the observations and described the mistakes as “inaccuracies” and “citation errors”. The Chamber found that the lawyer’s submissions contained a pattern of numerous, repeated, substantive errors rather than isolated citation mistakes and concluded that her conduct fell short of the professional and ethical duties imposed by the Court, duties that are also found in domestic law.
The Chamber submitted a reasoned proposal to the President of the Court that the lawyer be excluded from representing applicants before the Court for two years. The President approved that proposal.
