hn.title: Automatic Checking of Compiler Correctness with E-Graphs
hn.text:
Automatic Checking of Compiler Correctness with E-Graphs
A tricky domain for automated theorem proving
Adam Chlipala
Nov 17, 2026
9
2
Share
This article is crossposted between Prof. Adam Chlipala’s blog Structure and Guarantees and the blog of CSAIL , the MIT lab where the research being discussed took place.
I’m in the home stretch of a series of articles on constructing correct and efficient programs step-by-step using proven rewrite rules , which I argue is an important alternative to the ways AI coding agents are being used widely today. Previous examples have included tensor programs , digital hardware , and low-level cryptographic software . The last article introduced e-graphs, a data structure and set of related algorithms for efficiently exploring many alternative ways to write algebraic expressions. That technology has proven very useful for both program verification and program optimization.
Thanks for reading Structure and Guarantees! Subscribe for free to receive new posts and support my work.
I’m going to give an example now of this approach in action, in hot-off-the-presses research. Our paper to appear at POPL 2027 in January in Mexico City uses e-graphs to automate formal verification of compilers. It seems to be the first example of a general proof-automation tool that can take in a compiler definition for a new programming language the tool has never seen before, with no extra annotations meant just to guide theorem proving, and prove it correct automatically. (There are past examples that applied to fixed programming languages, as in Cobalt and Rhodium .) The final version of the paper isn’t quite posted as of this writing, but you can find the details in first author Dustin Jamner ’s PhD dissertation . Undergraduate Tilek Askerbekov also contributed to this paper.
What Kind of Compilers?
First I need to level with you about what kind of compiler we are talking about. It’s not one that looks especially like GCC or Clang , the canonical ways to resolve that word in industry. Instead, let me welcome you to the mathematically intriguing parallel universe of compilers for functional programming languages . The compilers our research project deals with follow in the tradition of classic research paper “From System F to Typed Assembly Language” . I’m not exactly an unbiased evaluator of this set of ideas, having done a postdoc with faculty author of the paper Greg Morrisett and undergraduate research with his former PhD advisor Bob Harper . Let’s take a quick look, though, at how this kind of compiler works. The idea is that compilation is broken into stages, and every intermediate form of a program is checked in a sound type system that guarantees lack of crashes, which is very different from classic compilers that quickly drop down to intermediate languages where all safety bets are off.
To avoid gratuitous dependencies on functional-programming lore, I’ll use an example program from Python , which we want to compile, gradually, until it becomes sufficiently like assembly language . Our starting program is a nice simple one.
def square(x):
return x * x
def compute(x):
return square(x + 1) + 3
print(compute(4)) Programmers generally take for granted the ability for one function to call another, which calls another, and so on. This freedom is usually implemented behind the scenes with a call stack . Our first compiler transformation will make the call stack explicit. In fact, the call stack will manifest as a chain of first-class functions , with each calling the function for the next lower level of the stack. This transformation is conversion to continuation-passing style , where we use “continuation” to refer to the functions we are introducing.
def square(x, k):
k(x * x)
def compute(x, k):
def after_square(y):
k(y + 3)
square(x + 1, after_square)
compute(4, print) Notice what happened: each function now takes a continuation k as an explicit argument. Where a function would have returned, it instead calls its continuation with the result. Now no function (beyond certain primitives) ever returns, which lines up well with how hardware execution actually works. The call stack was just an opt-in fiction that feels natural to us because our brains evolved to understand natural language with similar structure (a soap box I’ll climb back onto in a future article or two, to explain some downsides for practical programming of giving this fiction too much special status). This example also depends somewhat on tail-call optimization for its reasonableness, which Python doesn’t actually provide, but let’s imagine that it did.
What about this code is still too distant from what hardware can support directly? The function definition of after_square casually mentions a variable k from the enclosing scope . The term of art is that after_square is a lexical closure that captures variable k . This kind of mechanism is rather remote from what is natural to implement in hardware, so we also want a closure conversion compiler phase that removes use of captured variables, instead changing those variables into explicit function arguments, packaged up in first-class environments . The result for our running example is:
def invoke(closure, value):
code, env = closure
code(env, value)
def square(env, x, k):
invoke(k, x * x)
def after_square(env, y):
k = env["k"]
invoke(k, y + 3)
def compute(env, x, k):
continuation = (after_square, {"k": k})
square({}, x + 1, continuation)
def print_result(env, value):
print(value)
initial_continuation = (print_result, {})
compute({}, 4, initial_continuation) Every place a first-class function value appeared before, we now see an explicit closure , a pair of a function reference and an environment dictionary that packages up all of the captured variables that function is allowed to access. A useful property of this code is that all control flow , or code that determines which other code should run, now uses features that map fairly directly to assembly language. I

ChatGPT for SNES is an unofficial experiment designed by Benj Edwards and coded by AI agents: a ChatGPT-style chat program for the Super Nintendo. Its training conversations were written by gpt-oss-120b, OpenAI's open-weight model. Not made or endorsed by OpenAI.

Press Start (Enter) on the title screen, then type on your keyboard and press Enter to send. Each letter takes a moment to appear, because the page moves the cursor on the game's own on-screen keyboard.

hn.title: Do not buy RAM, compress
hn.text:
Do not buy RAM, compress!
19 Nov, 2026
AI has changed a lot. We do more work in parallel. This increases the memory demand on our workstations.
Also, memory is expensive and often not extendable. So buying more RAM is not an easy option.
Recently I was running out of memory, I found my solution in zram , a solution to compress memory.
Memory compression is not new. If you have a Windows or Mac device you are already using it.
Also, many Android smartphones utilize the technique of using compression to put more data into the RAM.
Unfortunately not all Linux environments have RAM compression enabled by default.
Fedora, Pop!_OS do, but Ubuntu doesn’t. Amazon Linux only enables zram on smaller virtual machines.
Most other distributions do not have it enabled.
Compressing memory does come with small, but not really noticeable, downsides. It takes a little bit more from your CPU and adds latency to some processes.
What you gain is gigantic amounts of extra capacity. It is not uncommon to see compression ratios up to 1:4.
I remember that in the early days of writing SaaS software we would often need double the size of the machines when we added more features to our monolithic app.
Often the CPUs were under little stress, so we could have avoided upgrading if we had enabled RAM compression.
This could have cut our Cloud spend in half!
How it looks in practice
I opened a lot of websites in Firefox. So many, it would almost fully take all system memory. (I have 32GB with some reserved for the graphics)

en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linux en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nederland \
imdb.com rottentomatoes.com archive.org nationalgeographic.com nasa.gov flickr.com/explore espn.com weather.com \
canva.com figma.com notion.so trello.com office.com dropbox.com wikihow.com ; do
firefox --new-tab "https:// $u " >/dev/null 2 > & 1 ; sleep 1
done
If we look at the running apps, then we see it should not fit.
In the memory usage we see that some demand was placed into the zram swap space.
In the terminal we can check how much memory is used, and we can calculate the compression ratio.
5.7G of data in 1.7G of RAM. That’s a compression ratio of 1:3.35.
Getting started with zram compression
Compressing RAM is something which helps to get you more out of your own hardware, but also out of your cloud environment.
Do more with less.
The Arch Linux wiki has a good article on how to get started .
Looking forward to hearing about your experiences.
Update (20 November 2026)
zram is nice, but zswap is better!
Yesterday the article got featured on Hacker News .
Nice to see the conversation and I hope that some of you started experimenting with compressing memory.
Making more efficient use of the available resources is something important to understand as a community.
Two articles were mentioned that I think are a very important addition.
While zram works fine for my situation, they advocate that zswap is the better option for most situations.
After reading both articles I agree with this conclusion.
So, I will be changing my configuration to use zswap instead.
Make sure to read the following:
I was wrong! zswap IS better than zram by Hayden James, in Blog Linux
Debunking zswap and zram myths by Chris Down

Garage Door Spam
hn.text:
Garage Door Spam
16 Nov, 2026
In the beginning, my garage door opener worked fine. When the door opened or closed, I would get a notification. If I'm away from home and the door opens, something weird is going down. The "myQ" app generally worked although it was encrusted with ads:
I continued using it because I trusted that notifications were meaningful...
...until recently (October 2026):
This is un-fucking-acceptable. As in, absolutely fucking not.
The manufacturer (Chamberlain) cut off third-party access to its APIs (via myQ) in late 2023. In response, I purchased a pair of ratgdo32 devices to opt out of the bullshit.
ratgdo is a WiFi control board for your garage door opener that works over your local network using ESP Home or HomeKit
The device is a ~$62 board from ratcloud llc running open-source firmware that wires to the opener's existing terminals and speaks LiftMaster's Security+ 2.0 protocol locally.
These were easy enough to hook up. I won't reproduce the instructions here.
The bundle included six black wires, an auxiliary harness I didn’t need.
My router hands each board a fixed address at 192.168.0.192 and 192.168.0.245. Apple's HomeKit just worked and I'm able to control them with voice commands: “Hey Siri, open Door 1”
When I was growing up, my father wired a mercury switch onto our garage door that lit up a light in the hallway when we'd left the garage door open. This was a valuable signal that helped our family avoid accidentally leaving the door open overnight. Since the ratgdo32 has a JSON status endpoint, I was able to rebuild Dad's solution in software with Slack:
The script runs at night checking for an open door:
*/10 21 -23,0-5 * * * garage-watch
The repo maintainer made my day when I submitted a tiny pull request : "Simple and useful. Happy to merge this. Thank you."
Both boards are now reachable over my Tailscale network, so my monitoring software can load /healthcheck. This required a custom route:
/Applications/Tailscale.app/Contents/MacOS/Tailscale set \
--advertise-routes = 192 .168.0.192/32,192.168.0.245/32
After approving the route, my monitoring software can verify the hardware is working.
Everything runs locally with no cloud, and notifications now say who opened the door which myQ never did.
To anyone at Chamberlain responsible for myQ, I offer my sincerest Fuck You.

Visited Links Are Purple
hn.text:
Visited links are purple
Monday
16 Nov
2026
A few weeks ago Kev Quirk asked: Do you use :visited on links? — and I said to myself: No! I don’t use visited links… but why don’t I use visited links?
TL;DR: I’ve gone and styled visited links, and they’re purple.
Blue and purple
I did a cursory five minutes of research and found Wikipedia still styles visited links (blue to purple). MDN does too. As does the GOV.UK design system — they have a special class to opt-out of the visited style. BBC News turns black links to grey, how emo.
I decided to style visited links within my <main> body copy. Which to be fair is most links but not the big headings on my blog index for example. I was too intimidated to turn those purple. Maybe you can give me the courage to style those too?
It looked a bit weird at first but I like the colourful additions to my blog.
Accessibility
WCAG 2.2 guidelines have no requirement to differentiate visited from unvisited links. Regardless, visited links should meet all the same criteria applied to any link.
There is one specific exception ( following this discussion ). Because web browsers have strict style limitations and technical constraints due to privacy concerns :
Where color alone distinguishes between visited and unvisited links, it does not result in a failure of this Success Criterion, even where the contrast between the two link colors is below 3:1.
SC 1.4.1 Use of Color (Level A)
This means that a subtle contrast different in blue vs purple is not considered an accessibility failure under that rule.
Web accessibility is all about ensuring a comparable experience for all users. Nothing can be perfectly accessible though. I think this small enhancement is fine, even if not everyone can see the difference. It’s a rare exception though. I’m conscious that too often excuses are made to ignore UX parity. I think any higher contrast or another visual indicator would be off-putting and impede readability. Forgoing any style doesn’t help anyone either. If blue and purple is good enough for those examples mentioned above, I’m on board.
Bryce Wray commented on Kev Quirk’s blog to note that Chromium browsers introduced :visited link partitioning in 2025. I had no idea this was a thing!
What do you think, do you care about visited link styles?
Bubbles
I found Kev Quirk’s blog on bubbles.town . Bubbles is a charming social RSS aggregator. It’s doing a great job at supporting small personal blogs and promoting non-toxic topics. Bubbles is far from perfect though. It probably needs a tech filter. It certainly needs more participation in comments and voting. The developer is actively working to improve the site and a community is growing, so that’s cool to see.
I hope Bubbles can thrive and remain human. This is the web we need to bypass the dead web Google et. al. are gatekeeping. Let them wall themselves in with their slop!

hn.title: Global stock markets slump as Anthropic's record IPO fails to stem AI sell-off
hn.text:
Shares in Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, were on Friday worth hardly more than when they listed. Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty Images
View image in fullscreen
Shares in Anthropic, which makes the Claude chatbot, were on Friday worth hardly more than when they listed. Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty Images
Anthropic shares slump on second day of trading as markets reel from AI sell-off
Nasdaq erases 2026 gains and Asian markets record worst week since 2020 as investors question huge sums being poured into AI build-out
Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
Anthropic’s shares fell at the start of its second day of trading, as its record-breaking IPO failed to stem a sell-off in AI-linked companies.
As they dropped, the wider stock market fell with them, with the Nasdaq Composite erasing all its gains for 2026. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 briefly entered correction territory.
Shares in the frontier AI company behind the Claude chatbot, which floated in the US on Thursday, fell by as much as 12% on Friday. They dropped to $85.12, towards the $83 level at which Anthropic priced its stock market debut.
Anthropic’s first two days as a listed company have been volatile. Its shares jumped by 17% on Thursday, after briefly surging by almost 40% when trading in the firm began.
Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn?
Read more
US technology stocks followed Anthropic down on Friday, knocking 2.9% off the value of the Nasdaq share index, with the memory chipmaker SanDisk falling 14% and rival Micron down 12%. The broader S&P 500 share index fell 1.66% in morning trading in New York.
Neil Wilson, a UK investor strategist at Saxo, said there was “just relentless selling in tech”. He warned: “Anthropic shares tumbled -12% to take an $85 handle as the post-IPO euphoria gives way to the reality of a steep sell-off across the tech and AI space that shows no sign of easing just yet.”
Global markets slumped on Friday too; Asian stock markets recorded their worst week since 2020, as shares in big chip companies fell. In Taiwan, stocks dropped 6.7% to hit their lowest point since mid-April, with the chip maker TSMC down about 6%.
The scale of the decline in Taiwan prompted the chair of its stock exchange to pledge to ensure the stable operation ⁠of capital markets, and reassure investors they should remain confident in the fundamentals of Taiwanese companies.
In Japan, the Nikkei index fell 5%, while South Korea’s tech-heavy Kospi index lost 5.5%. Shares in the tech investor SoftBank had their worst day in more than two years, down 14.5% in Tokyo, amid worries around its aggressive bets on AI.
European stock markets posted their biggest weekly loss since March 2025, with the pan-European Stoxx 600 dropping 1.9% on Friday. London’s blue-chip stock index hit a five-month low.
The sell-off followed losses on Wall Street on Thursday, where the main indices all fell by more than 2% on a day dominated by Anthropic’s IPO .
View image in fullscreen
South Korea’s Kospi index lost 5.5% at end of trading. Photograph: Yonhap/EPA Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at the investing and trading platform IG, said Anthropic could be “draining market liquidity”, as investors sell shares in other companies to raise funds to pay for stock in the newly floated AI firm.
“The slide from yesterday’s highs sends a message that there might be more at work here than investors realise, and while brokers are scrambling to buy more, that liquidity has to come from somewhere, and the other tech names may be the first ones to feel the pressure,” Beauchamp said.
skip past newsletter promotion
after newsletter promotion
Anthropic’s flotation has failed to ease worries around the AI trade, as investors increasingly question whether companies can deliver the returns necessary to justify the billions of dollars being poured into the AI build out.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said: “The IPO demonstrated that demand for AI exposure remains strong, but it has not been enough to overcome concerns about elevated valuations, profitability and the sustainability of investment spending.
“The broader market mood has shifted from buying the dip towards questioning whether the correction has further to run. The weakness in equal-weighted indices suggests that selling pressure is no longer confined to a handful of technology giants, while Europe’s recent outperformance has also faded.”
Nvidia shares fell by 7% after California served the chip company with a subpoena as part of an investigation into whether its advanced semiconductors ended up in China.
Britain’s FTSE 100 share index dropped by 5.1% this week, its biggest weekly fall since the start of the Iran war.
Fears that US central bankers may raise interest rates to fight inflation have lifted the dollar to a 19-month high, and pushed down the gold price – with gold on track for its worst week since March.
Bitcoin hit its lowest level in four months, dropping below the $60,000 point for the first time since early July.

hn.title: Jujutsu Primer
hn.text:
Jujutsu Primer
November 18, 2026
This guide is a brief(ish) introduction to the Jujutsu ( jj ) version control system (VCS) for someone familiar with Git.
Why try Jujutsu?
jj provides primitives for version control that are simple to learn, but elegantly compose into powerful workflows. Features like automatic rebase and native undo soften the sharp edges of Git. Eventually, you’ll organically discover new powerful workflows that would be too cumbersome to attempt with most other VCS tools.
If you work in a Git repository, you can try it today. Jujutsu and Git can be used side-by-side in the same repository , so you can try out jj on a git repo on your own, without fully ejecting from git .
Personally, I think jj considerably boosts my effectiveness, because it allows me to keep VCS bookkeeping out of my working memory. Automatic rebasing also makes stacked diff workflows quite easy, and reduces thrashing of my working memory. It’s also just a fun tool to use.
Installing jj
Official installation instructions are here , but here are a few common methods:
# macOS
brew install jj
# Arch Linux
pacman - S jujutsu
# NixOS (ideally from nixpkgs-unstable)
nix-shell - p jujutsu
# From source
# (Requires a recent Rust and ~/.cargo/bin on your PATH)
cargo install -- locked -- bin jj jj-cli
Setup and configuration
In an existing git repository, run:
jj git init
From here on, jj and git repo state will be synchronized automatically.
To set your user details globally, run commands like these:
jj config set -- user user.name " Some One "
jj config set -- user user.email " someone@example.com "
You can edit jj ’s TOML configuration for your user in an editor with:
jj config edit -- user
In addition to the --user scope, jj config also has --repo and --workspace scopes. View the merged config with:
jj config list
Commits and changes
A commit , also called a revision , is essentially the same thing as a git commit. It represents a snapshot of repository state that descends from one or more parent repository snapshots. It is often visualized as a diff against a singular parent commit, or in the case of a merge commit, the diff against multiple parent commits once merged.
When using a Git repo backend, the jj commit ID is the same as the git commit ID: a hash formatted as a hex string. In the output of jj log below, the hex hashes 2bea5e3d and 849165bc on the right are commit IDs.
$ jj log
@ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc
│ (empty) (no description set)
◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d
│ Adjust config
~
The IDs on the left hand side ( royxmykx and kpqxywon ) are change IDs , which are stable identifiers for logical changes as they physically evolve over time. We’ll discuss these more in the next section.
Commit IDs and change IDs can be referenced in shorthand with an unambiguous (unique) prefix. jj helpfully highlights the shortest unique prefix of most IDs to make it easy to type them manually. For example,
instead of copying and pasting kpqxywon , we can type in a prefix, down to the shortest unique prefix k .
We can inspect the commit 2bea5e3d with jj show , using its short prefix 2 .
$ jj show 2
Commit ID: 2bea5e3d1992a60ba9ee52c6ce37c55adba9e8fb
Change ID: royxmykxtrkrqppotnrvutxlvrvqyxmy
Bookmarks: main main@git main@origin
Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:10:46 )
Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:10:46 )
Adjust config
diff --git a/config.py b/config.py
index 7366a4e31d..174ffea06b 100644
--- a/config.py
+++ b/config.py
@@ -1,1 +1,1 @@
-DEFAULT_LIMIT = 10
+DEFAULT_LIMIT = 20
Many folks configure a custom diff formatter, like Delta . See configuration docs if you’re interested.
Creating & evolving changes
Let’s take another look at our commit graph:
$ jj log
@ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:17:12 8 49165bc
│ (empty) (no description set)
◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d
│ Adjust config
~
On commit 849165bc , you’ll see the symbol @ on the graph node. This represents a snapshot of our working copy , or the code we have actually checked out in our local directory. We can inspect this special commit pointer in a variety of ways:
jj show shows commit details and a diff, which is empty here.
$ jj show
Commit ID: 849165bca19639dbd6ccb53e8c1340e78c36d59a
Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk
Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:17:12 )
Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:17:12 )
(no description set)
jj status shows repo state with diff stats.
$ jj status
The working copy has no changes.
Working copy (@) : k pqxywon 8 49165bc (empty) (no description set)
Parent commit (@-): r oyxmykx 2 bea5e3d main | Adjust config
jj diff works much like git diff . Its output is empty here, since there are no changes in the current working copy relative to the parent commit.
$ jj diff
This output isn’t very interesting, since @ has no changes. Let’s make an example change to see what happens. If we edit main.py and rerun jj show , we see this:
$ jj show
Commit ID: 66b59f20c534705cfb753c722222290e9185b22c
Change ID: kpqxywonksrltlrkyqukqqsxpltznztk
Author : Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:26:43 )
Committer: Ethan Lowman < ethan@example.com > ( 2026-11-15 12:26:43 )
(no description set)
diff --git a/main.py b/main.py
new file mode 100644
index 0000000000..c74cd2e0e0
--- /dev/null
+++ b/main.py
@@ -0,0 +1,2 @@ def my_new_feature():
+ def my_new_feature():
+ pass
$ jj log
@ k pqxywon ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:26:43 6 6b59f20
│ (no description set)
◆ r oyxmykx ethan@example.com 2026-11-15 12:10:46 main 2 bea5e3d
│ Adjust config
~
You’ll notice several things have changed. The working copy has been automatically committed, and @ is no longer marked (empty) . The new commit ID for @ is 66b59f20 , since we’ve added changes, but the change ID for 66b59f20 is still kpqxywon . jj has no staging area like in

hn.title: Rebuilding my local voice assistant pipeline
hn.text:
Rebuilding my voice assistant pipeline
https://blog.platypush.tech/article/Rewriting-my-voice-assistant-pipeline
📝
Swapping openwakeword for microwakeword and making voice detection smarter
Fabio Manganiello
Nov 19, 2026
#platypush
#voice
#voiceassistant
#microwakeword
#openai
Wake word detection: a new assistant.microwakeword plugin
Speech-to-text: assistant.openai, with a much better ear
Responses and context: the openai plugin
Text-to-speech: tts.openai
The full configuration
What changed on the code side
Caveats
I wrote an article a couple of months ago describing how I rebuilt my old voice assistant pipeline in Platypush .
And I wrote earlier articles describing my journey through self-hosted voice assistants - in 2024 (with Picovoice ), in 2020 (diving into the legacy assistant.google integration, the now defunct assistant.alexa integration, the now defunct Snowboy integration, the now defunct DeepSpeech integration and Picovoice) and the original article in 2019 describing the Google Assistant integration.
For a couple of months I used the voice pipeline described in my latest article as my main driver, but after getting used to the robustness of commercial voice assistants I was unhappy with the high rates of false positives/negatives of my self-hosted pipeline, as well as its lack of robustness in detecting start/end of speech, especially in noisy environments and using cheap microphones.
After a bit of experimentation, I decided to swap and fine tune a few parts, and after a couple of days of trying the results are satisfying enough for me to write a short article about it.
The resulting pipeline is:
Wake word detection: a new assistant.microwakeword plugin
Until recently I used assistant.openwakeword , which wraps openWakeWord .
It works, but the project has been quiet for a while and all of its pre-trained models are v0.1 files from 2023, mostly trained on synthetic speech.
In practice I was getting both false positives (the hotword triggering on background noise) and false negatives (the hotword not detected unless I was close to the microphone).
I added a new plugin, assistant.microwakeword , on top of microWakeWord through the pymicro-wakeword Python bindings.
microWakeWord is the engine used by ESPHome and Home Assistant Voice, its models are actively maintained, and the built-in models ( okay_nabu , hey_jarvis , hey_mycroft , alexa ) ship with the package — no download required.
The current official models are provided under the ESPHome micro-wake-word-models repository .
Custom models are supported too: drop a microWakeWord JSON manifest (with its .tflite model) in the plugin's models directory and reference it by name.
The plugin exposes the same API as assistant.openwakeword (same models , detection_threshold , frame_duration , patience_frames , input_device , input_volume parameters, same list_models action, same HotwordDetectedEvent ), so switching is a matter of just changing the configuration to point to the new plugin:
assistant.microwakeword :
models :
- alexa
A few design notes:
Without an explicit detection_threshold , each model uses the probability_cutoff from its own manifest (0.9 for alexa ), which is the value the model was validated against.
Models already smooth their output over a sliding window, so unlike openwakeword, patience_frames defaults to 0 here.
The audio thread never touches the TFLite models directly: it queues frames (and a reset marker) to the main thread, because MicroWakeWord.reset() reloads the interpreter and isn't safe to call concurrently.
Like assistant.openwakeword , the plugin releases the audio device when another assistant plugin starts a conversation, and re-acquires it when the conversation ends.
Speech-to-text: assistant.openai , with a much better ear
assistant.openai records audio when a conversation starts and transcribes it through Whisper.
The tricky part has always been end-of-speech detection : knowing when the user has finished talking. The previous implementation used a per-frame boolean from WebRTC VAD, and any single frame classified as speech would reset the silence timer. With even a bit of background noise, phrases would only end when the maximum conversation duration was hit.
The audio preprocessing layer ( AudioPreprocessor , shared by the STT integrations) has been reworked:
Silero VAD as the primary backend (through onnxruntime , no PyTorch required), with WebRTC VAD and a plain RMS-based detector as fallbacks. To get an idea of Silero VAD's performance compared against other solutions for speech activity detection, take a look at the insightful article One voice detector to rule them all . The Silero model is downloaded on first use into the Platypush workdir and checksum-verified:
assistant.openai :
# auto = silero -> webrtc -> energy, depending on what's installed
vad_backend : auto
Hysteresis + sliding window : a frame becomes speech above the VAD threshold and stays speech until its score drops by a margin, and the per-frame decisions are smoothed by majority vote over a 0.5s window. A single noise burst can no longer keep a conversation alive.
Adaptive noise floor : the background noise level is tracked over time, and frames that aren't louder than noise_floor_factor (default 2.0, ~6 dB) times the floor are never considered as speech.
On a synthetic benchmark (Piper-generated phrases mixed with babble and burst noise), the old settings kept conversations open for 6–10 seconds after the speech had ended; the new pipeline ends them 1.0–1.6 seconds after the last word, which is the configured conversation_end_timeout plus the smoothing lag.
Since the changes on Platypush have been performed directly in the AudioPreprocessor also used by other native speech-to-text engines, other speech-to-text plugins also benefit from them - e.g. if you use assistant.vosk for full on-device detection.
Responses and context: the openai plugin
The transcribed phrase is processed by the openai plugin, which handles both th

The offering consisted of 1,103,351,354 shares sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares sold by certain selling stockholders. The aggregate gross proceeds from the offering, before deducting underwriting discounts and commissions and other offering expenses, were approximately $93.5 billion, of which approximately $91.6 billion was received by Anthropic. Anthropic did not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders.

google.title: A game you cannot win unless you have a quantum computer
google.text:
A game you cannot win unless you have a quantum computer
November 19, 2026
Shashwat Kumar and Rodrigo Cortiñas, Research Scientists, Google Quantum AI, Google Research
On a superconducting processor, we turned one of quantum mechanics’ strangest features into something you can measure, benchmark, and put to work across systems as large as 105 qubits.
Quick links
Paper
Share
Copy link
×
Here is a Sunday paper-style puzzle you can try right now. Draw a 3×3 grid. Fill every cell with either +1 or −1, subject to two rules: each row must multiply to +1, and each column must multiply to −1.
Go ahead. We’ll wait…
You didn’t manage it, right? There is an elegant reason for that. For a row to multiply to +1, it needs an even number of −1s. For a column to multiply to −1, it needs an odd number. Add up the rows and you learn the grid contains an even number of −1s. Add up the columns and you learn it contains an odd number. Well…That’s impossible!
The grid would have to be two contradictory things at once. No such table exists; it is a paradox.
Now turn the puzzle into a game: Each round, Alice is handed a row and Bob a column. Without talking, Alice fills her row by the row rule and Bob fills his column by the column rule. They win if they put the same number in the square where their row and column intersect. Any plan made in advance is just a pre-written table, meaning at best they will win 8 out of 9 rounds. This changes if they use a quantum computer. It won't fill in the impossible grid, but in principle, it lets them win every round.
The reason is a property called quantum contextuality , arguably the strangest feature of quantum mechanics. Einstein once famously asked whether the moon is there when nobody looks, his way of insisting that physical properties ought to exist whether or not anyone measures them. For quantum systems, contextuality is the precise, experimentally testable statement that the answer can be no: you cannot assign fixed, pre-existing values to everything you might measure.
What a measurement yields can depend on which other compatible measurements you make alongside it (i.e., on its context ). This is not only a deep philosophical statement, but more so, cutting-edge science and the basis of a new technology. And in the game above, Alice and Bob can use it to engineer a solution. Their answers are not looked up in a hidden table written in advance; the table does not exist. Their answers come into being as they measure, and quantum correlations stitch them together more tightly than any classical rulebook permits.
Entanglement usually gets top billing as the “magic ingredient” of quantum computing. But a growing body of theory suggests contextuality is the deeper resource, the thing that actually powers certain quantum algorithms past their classical counterparts. The catch is that, until recently, contextuality had been demonstrated almost exclusively in small systems of a few particles. Whether it survives, and stays useful, in the many-body systems that real quantum computers are made of was an open question.
That is the question we set out to answer. In " Quantum-classical separation in bounded-resource tasks arising from measurement contextuality ," published in Science , we demonstrate and measure contextuality on our superconducting quantum processors. Our qubits win the magic square game 98.3% of the time, exceed the classical limit on a contextuality test, and outperform classical strategies in tasks spanning up to 105 qubits. Along the way, these tasks proved to be a sensitive new benchmark for quantum hardware, catching subtle errors that random-circuit tests miss.
Beating the classical bound
We ran what is commonly called the magic square game on our Willow quantum processor. Alice and Bob each hold two qubits, sharing two entangled Bell pairs instead of a pre-written table, and measure them using preset settings for their assigned row or column to get their ±1 entries.
The best conceivable classical strategy loses at least one round in nine, winning at most 88.89% of the time. When we played all nine versions of the game 100,000 times apiece, our qubits lost roughly one in sixty, winning 98.30% of them (0.9830 ± 0.0001).
The gap is meaningful and statistically significant: our qubits coordinated better than any pre-written table allows. That's because no cell has a value fixed in advance. Each answer takes shape only when it is measured alongside the rest of its row or column (its context), and shared entanglement makes Alice's and Bob's answers for the shared cell agree.
With shared entanglement and a prearranged measurement plan, Alice and Bob can in principle agree at the intersection in every round. On our hardware, noise causes about one loss in 60.
Putting a number on contextuality
The magic square game demonstrated the potential power of contextuality, so next we set out to measure how contextual a machine is. We used a Bell–Kochen–Specker inequality , closely related to the famous Bell test which showed that entangled particles like the Bell pairs above can't carry answers fixed in advance. Our inequality bundles a set of correlations into a single number, χ . In terms of the rows and columns from the game above it reads, χ = R1 + R2 + R3 − C1 − C2 − C3, where R and C represent the products of the rows and columns Alice and Bob had to calculate earlier:
+1
+1
+1
R1 = (+1)*(+1)*(+1) = +1
+1
−1
−1
R2 = (+1)*(−1)*(−1) = +1
−1
+1
−1
R3 = (−1)*(+1)*(−1) = +1
C1 = (+1)*(+1)*(−1) = −1
C2 = (+1)*(−1)*(+1) = −1
C3 = (+1)*(−1)*(−1) = +1
χ = 4
Any universe where measurement outcomes are predetermined must obey χ ≤ 4 (try a few tables and you will see that χ can only take values -4, 0, and 4). Quantum mechanics permits values up to 6, which can only happen if all Rs = +1 and all Cs = -1. And unlike most such tests, this one is state-independent : it doesn’t matter how you prepare the qubits, which makes it a property of the machine rather than of a carefully

nvidia.title: NVIDIA and Microsoft Expand Accelerated Computing From Azure to Windows PCs
nvidia.summary: NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs. At Microsoft Ignite, the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to […]
nvidia.text:
NVIDIA and Microsoft are extending their full-stack collaboration to help organizations build, customize and deploy intelligent applications — from next-generation infrastructure on Azure to industrial systems and Windows PCs.
At Microsoft Ignite , the companies are expanding access to Azure virtual machines powered by NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems, as well as adding customer availability to NVIDIA open models and customization capabilities through Microsoft Foundry, and new options for running AI at the edge, where businesses generate and use their data.
Microsoft is also using NVIDIA technologies to accelerate its own models and services, including NVIDIA Dynamo inference software for post-training and NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs for Bing search models.
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 Running in Azure
NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72 systems are running in Azure data centers , providing infrastructure designed for demanding reasoning, agentic applications, and large-scale model training and inference.
Microsoft and NVIDIA are also collaborating to extend confidential computing to bare-metal and rack-scale AI infrastructure. The work will help protect sensitive models and data while they are being processed, supporting organizations that need to work with proprietary or regulated information.
NVIDIA Confidential Computing and attestation help customers verify the computing environment before releasing sensitive models, data or keys. As AI workloads span more interconnected accelerators, the companies are working to extend those protections across the AI factory infrastructure.
To help data centers get more performance from available power, NVIDIA and Microsoft are also collaborating on power efficiency using NVIDIA MaxLPS .
Azure’s Vera Rubin preview builds on NVIDIA and Microsoft’s codesign and performance optimization, underscored in the latest NVIDIA Blackwell-based MLPerf results. In MLPerf Training v6.1 , Azure scaled to 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 NVL72 systems on the DeepSeek-V3 model, the largest scale in the round. In MLPerf Inference v6.1 , Azure’s NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 systems led cloud submissions on DeepSeek-R1 interactive throughput by over 10%, per Signal65.
Helping Enterprises Customize and Deploy Open Models
Enterprise AI agents need to reason through complex tasks, find relevant company information and understand business documents. NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding the models and services available through Microsoft Foundry to help developers bring these capabilities into business applications.
Microsoft’s serverless Programmed Training offering gives developers control over post-training workflows while Foundry manages the underlying infrastructure. Enterprises can focus on their business data, evaluating model responses and improving model behavior.
Foundry Managed Compute adds support for deploying custom model weights, helping connect model customization with deployment through Microsoft’s managed services.
EY used Programmed Training in Microsoft Foundry to adapt NVIDIA Nemotron open models for classifying corporate purchasing records, improving accuracy on its evaluation dataset by 55% and lowering cost by 15x compared with proprietary frontier models. The work demonstrates how enterprises can customize open models for specialized business tasks.
The expanded NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 lineup on Foundry Managed Compute supports different requirements across enterprise applications. Nemotron 3.5 Super is designed for long-running agents working across coding, research and business workflows, while Lightning supports applications that need fast responses and tool use.
Complementary models help agents find relevant information with Nemotron Embed and Rerank, extract structured information from documents with Nemotron Parse and detect harmful content with Nemotron Content Safety. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt — designed for high-throughput, low-latency reasoning — and Transcribe, for speech recognition, are coming soon.
Bringing AI Closer to Enterprise Data
NVIDIA and Microsoft are expanding deployment options beyond the cloud, helping organizations run models and agents closer to their data while maintaining control over their infrastructure and operations.
Expanded support for Nemotron 3.5 in Foundry Local brings capabilities for reasoning, coding and tool-using agents to Azure Local environments. Retrieval models help applications find evidence across text, document images, charts and tables.
Azure Local will also support NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPUs from hardware partners, giving organizations additional options for deploying AI on premises.
Azure Local is expanding to NVIDIA Jetson Thor and Jetson Orin edge AI platforms to support industrial applications such as machine vision, robotics and autonomous operations. NVIDIA physical AI models, including Cosmos , are also being brought to Foundry Local.
On Windows PCs powered by NVIDIA RTX Spark , NVIDIA and Microsoft will showcase local large language model experiences at Ignite, demonstrating how developers can run AI applications directly on devices.
For organizations using Cloud PCs, the companies are bringing Direct Stream capabilities to GPU-accelerated Windows 365 Cloud PCs. These capabilities support demanding graphics applications with up to two 4K streams at 60 frames per second and low latency, even over challenging networks. A limited preview is open for sign-ups, with public preview planned for early 2027.
Connecting Scientific AI With Microsoft Discovery
For scientific research, NVIDIA BioNemo Agent Toolkit and NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit are expanding into the Microsoft Discovery catalog , bringing models for life sciences, drug discovery and materials and chemical science into Microsoft’s agentic research platform.
BioNeMo Agent Toolkit helps scientists use natural language to run computational biology workflows in Microsoft Discovery, with agents coordinating the tools and model calls needed to carry out the work.

Save 30% on the first six-month term of a Performance or Ultimate membership. Big gaming plans, smaller price tag. Keep the holiday savings going: Check out more NVIDIA holiday deals for gamers, […]
nvidia.text:
GeForce NOW is kicking off Black Friday with more reasons to make time for gaming. Six-month memberships are back for a limited time. Save 30% on the first six-month term of a Performance or Ultimate membership . Big gaming plans, smaller price tag.
Keep the holiday savings going: Check out more NVIDIA holiday deals for gamers, creators and AI enthusiasts.
The living room gets a little more playtime, too. GeForce NOW arrives on Amazon Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K Select and Fire TV Stick 4K (2026 model) running Vega OS, alongside an Amazon offer launching later today for 90% off the first month of an eligible Performance or Ultimate membership in participating countries. It brings console-style gaming to the TV, straight from the Amazon cart.
Bethesda fans have more in store, with five favorites adding GOG support as part of nine games joining GeForce NOW this week.
Big RTX Power, Black Friday Price
Thousands of games are calling from the cloud.
Six-month Performance and Ultimate memberships are back for Black Friday, with 30% off the first six months for new memberships and eligible upgrades in select regions. The sale runs through Monday, Nov. 30, while supplies last.
Go Ultimate for GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, Steam Deck and other supported handhelds, browsers, mobile devices, compatible TVs and more . Sessions lasting up to eight hours and first-priority server access leave more room for marathon play.
Ultimate brings the latest NVIDIA innovations to the cloud, including DLSS 5 technology with the 3D-Guided Neural Rendering feature for lifelike lighting and materials in NBA 2K27 and Hogwarts Legacy , with support coming to War Thunder and Where Winds Meet .
The experience goes big with streaming at up to 5K resolution or up to 360 frames per second, plus high dynamic range, ultrawide support and saved in-game settings. DLSS Super Resolution, Multi Frame Generation and Ray Reconstruction enhance supported games, including the path-traced missions of 007 First Light and the reality-bending action of CONTROL Resonant , while NVIDIA Reflex and Cloud G-SYNC technologies help keep gameplay responsive and smooth.
GeForce NOW handles downloads, patches and updates for Ready-to-Play games, freeing local storage and leaving more time for gaming. Choose a membership and start the season streaming.
More Screens, Major Savings
Press play on more possibilities.
GeForce NOW officially expands to all three of Amazon’s Vega OS streaming media players including Fire TV Stick HD, Fire TV Stick 4K Select and Fire TV Stick 4K (2026 model) bringing thousands of supported games to more another screens in the home. Vega OS keeps Fire TV fast and responsive, so launching GeForce NOW and jumping into games feels quick and snappy, with no console required.
Getting started is simple: download the GeForce NOW app on a supported Fire TV device , sign in and connect a compatible controller. From cozy stories to epic adventures, turn-based tactics to co-op challenges, there’s plenty to build, explore and share with friends — all from the comfort of the couch.
There’s a fire deal to get the games going, too. Launching later today through Thursday, Dec. 31, get 90% off the first month of a Performance or Ultimate membership purchased directly through Amazon on supported Fire TV devices in participating regions. The cloud is ready. The next quest is calling.
GOG Big or Go Home
Five favorite worlds. Extra ways to play.
Five Bethesda titles expand their GeForce NOW support this week with their GOG versions: Indiana Jones and the Great Circle , Fallout 4 , The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim , DOOM and DOOM Eternal .
Uncover an ancient mystery in Indiana Jones and the Great Circle , a first-person adventure set between Raiders of the Lost Ark and The Last Crusade . Explore the wasteland in Fallout 4 or trade the Pip-Boy for dragons and open-world fantasy in The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim .
For a faster change of pace, DOOM brings relentless enemies, destructive weapons and fast-moving first-person combat, while its sequel, DOOM Eternal , turns up the intensity as the Slayer takes on demonic forces.
Members who own the newly supported GOG versions can stream those titles through GeForce NOW without purchasing them again. From treasure hunts to dragon hunts, the collection can follow across nearly any supported device. Familiar worlds, with a little more room to roam.
Members can look for the following games joining the GeForce NOW library this week:
Volvy’s Adventure: Reslimed (New release on Steam , Nov. 19)
Baldur’s Gate 3 ( Xbox Play Anywhere)
DOOM (2016) ( GOG )
DOOM Eternal ( GOG )
Fallout 4 ( GOG )
Graveyard Keeper 2 ( Epic Games Store and GOG )
Indiana Jones and the Great Circle ( GOG )
Moon Sweepers ( Steam )
The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Anniversary Edition ( GOG )
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.
Make it a cloud gaming weekend. Grab a day pass to try Performance or Ultimate before committing to a monthly membership, with the day pass cost applicable toward that first month.
What’s on the big-screen gaming lineup this weekend? Let us know on X or in the comments below.

nvidia.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark Compact Desktops Out Now
nvidia.summary: New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC. With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development […]
nvidia.text:
New NVIDIA RTX Spark compact desktops from ASUS, Dell and MSI are available today, bringing local AI agents, image and video generation, and model fine-tuning to a dedicated Windows PC.
With up to 128GB of unified memory and NVIDIA’s AI software stack, these systems provide room for larger local models alongside RTX-accelerated creative and development tools. A dedicated desktop can keep agents and scheduled tasks running while a laptop travels or handles other work.
Alongside the new desktops, an expanding software ecosystem brings more creative and development workflows to RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops.
Native Windows on Arm applications from Adobe, the NVIDIA DLSS Ray Reconstruction feature in Blender and local generation workflows in ComfyUI expand what creators and developers can do on RTX Spark — all on one Windows PC.
A Windows PC Built for Local AI
As workflows expand to include local AI models and agents, more work can continue beyond an active editing session — from generating assets to processing long renders or scheduled tasks.
RTX Spark compact desktops give developers, creators and AI enthusiasts a dedicated Windows PC for local models and always-on agents. They bring together image and video generation, model fine-tuning, creative applications and development tools in one compact system.
Running supported models locally keeps locally processed code and files on the PC and avoids per-token cloud application programming interface (API) charges for those tasks.
RTX Spark compact desktops like the ASUS ProArt GR1X mini PC are built to run personal AI agents 24/7.
RTX Spark desktops are equipped with a 20-core NVIDIA Grace CPU, an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU with 6,144 CUDA cores and up to 128GB of unified memory, delivering up to 1 petaflop of AI performance. Ten-gigabit Ethernet connectivity enables fast transfers of large datasets, model files and creative assets between RTX Spark compact desktops and networked storage.
This advanced hardware unlocks incredible capabilities for creators, developers and AI enthusiasts, including:
Running massive 120-billion-parameter large language models locally
Rendering 90GB+ 3D scenes in real time
Smoothly editing 4:2:2 video in real time
The MSI EdgeMesa N AI+ Series RTX Spark compact desktop.
New compact desktops are available for purchase from ASUS, Dell and MSI, joining the RTX Spark family of laptops available today. Mini PCs from Acer, GIGABYTE and HP are coming soon, along with the Microsoft Surface RTX Spark Dev Box .
From Local Agents to AI Creation
Native CUDA support and Linux development tools through Windows Subsystem for Linux give developers a foundation for building and running local AI workflows. Developers can set up agents with Hermes Agent or NVIDIA NemoClaw blueprints and fine-tune supported models using Unsloth.
RTX Spark can run creative agents that connect familiar applications and local AI tools, helping creators move from an idea to finished work with natural-language instructions.
NVIDIA Switchyard, now available in Hermes, automatically routes agent tasks between local and cloud models. Everyday tasks can run on device, while advanced reasoning draws on cloud models, helping manage cloud costs across creative workflows.
These capabilities come together in creative workflows that connect Photoshop and ComfyUI through Hermes Agent. Using natural-language instructions, creators can turn sketches into rendered images and animations, or animate an image entirely on device by isolating a subject and defining its motion.
NVIDIA brought these workflows to life at Adobe MAX, where attendees used natural-language instructions to turn sketches into rendered images and generate video for a shared digital Miami landscape.
The RTX Video Frame Generation and RTX Video HDR features, already available in ComfyUI, extend the pipeline: a generated clip can be expanded to 60 frames per second and converted to high dynamic range for color grading, all within a single ComfyUI workflow on RTX Spark.
Adobe Accelerates the Full Creative Stack for RTX Spark
NVIDIA and Adobe are expanding native Windows on Arm support and RTX acceleration across Adobe’s creative applications, helping video editors, photographers, designers and 3D artists work more efficiently on RTX Spark.
Adobe Premiere accelerates a range of AI-powered editing features through NVIDIA TensorRT-RTX , including Enhance Speech, Object Mask, Scene Edit Detection and Auto Reframe — so editors spend less time waiting and more time cutting.
GPU acceleration also extends to Film Impact transition and effects plug-ins. The update improves support for professional video formats, including Canon RAW, Red RAW, ARRI RAW, ARRICORE, ARRI HDE, H.264 and HEVC in MXF, ProRes RAW and long-GOP video. This lets editors realize more than 50% quicker turnaround on everyday H.264 video deliverables.
Adobe Photoshop adds TensorRT-RTX acceleration for the Remove Tool and ArmRTX Spark-native Camera Raw support, helping photographers remove unwanted objects faster and work with RAW images without relying on emulation. At Adobe MAX, Adobe previewed a next-generation image processing engine with extensive GPU acceleration, including interactive Gaussian blur and Light Leaks filters.
Adobe Substance 3D Painter 12.2 is now optimized for RTX Spark with native support on Arm for the first time in public beta. Artists in games, visual effects and visualization can run Substance Painter natively on RTX Spark laptops and compact desktops, with no compatibility layer required.
Adobe Illustrator and InDesign now offer native Windows on Arm versions optimized for RTX Spark. Adobe Illustrator delivers up to 30% higher performance than its emulated version, helping accelerate illustration, graphic design and page-layout workflows on RTX Spark.
Blender 5.3 Adds DLSS Ray Reconstruction to the Viewport
Blender 5.3 integrates DLSS 4.5 Ray Reconstruction into the Cycles viewport, helping artists evaluate light
